item.title: “I Yelled at the Top of My Lungs ‘He’s Alive!'”: How Two Kayakers Saved a Missing Hiker in One of America’s Most Remote National Parks
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine Score: 2.80
Isle Royale (Photo: Layne Kennedy / Corbis Documentary via Getty) An extensive missing hiker search in Michigan’s Upper Peninsula ended up concluding by chance this week when two kayakers crossed paths with a 70-year-old man who had been lost for 11 days. Craig Berg, of Royal Oak, Michigan, was reported overdue on September 6 in Isle Royale National Park after a planned multi-day hike. When family members alerted park officials to Berg’s status, an intensive search operation commenced. Search teams deployed ground resources, canine-assisted searches, boats, aircraft, and drones to locate Berg, but were still empty-handed as of Sep. 11. On Saturday, two paddlers chanced upon Berg near Intermediate Lake, more than a mile from established trails in the area. The group relayed Berg’s location to rescue crews, and a Coast Guard team soon arrived in a MH-60 Jayhawk to hoist him to safety. Berg was alert when found, according to the National Park Service, and was recovering well under medical care in Marquette, Michigan. His son, Evan Berg, recounted the moment he learned his father was alive to Detroit Local 4 news. “I yelled at the top of my lungs, ‘he’s alive!’” Berg said. “Wonderful feeling. [When I spoke to him], he was definitely shaken up; he was rattled. But he said, ‘man, I have enough stories for you to fill a book.’” The recent retiree and father of two dreamed of hiking the Appalachian Trail, according to Local 4, and had been focusing on shorter objectives such as the outing at Isle Royale. The adventure went sideways when he fell into a marsh, his son said, losing his wallet and phone. According to the Coast Guard, he was reportedly hypothermic and injured when the kayakers found him. Officials with the Park Service and the Michigan State Police were unavailable for comment as of this writing. In a statement, the Park Service acknowledged the large group of public and private teams that coordinated on the rescue. “The successful outcome reflects the combined efforts of search teams, partner agencies and members of the public who assisted throughout the operation,” the agency said. In a statement posted to Facebook on Thursday, Berg’s wife, Debbie, had a message for the adventurers who found him. “To the two gentlemen kayakers, who were National Guard from Saginaw and Metro D, who found him, my husband would like to buy you a beer,” she wrote. “Say when. “

item.title: Deep in the West’s Backcountry, These 6 Trails Lead to Sacred Rock Art and Ruins
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine Score: 2.02
(Photo: Josh Ewing/Getty Images) Every hike has a story to tell, but there’s something special about a trail that takes you to ancient dwellings or rock art. It forces the past into perspective. You visualize the people who existed there, walking the same trails, planting food in the surrounding fields, and imagine how they might have lived. I geek out over archeological and cultural heritage hikes. They make the hike itself feel more like a quest than just a stroll through nature. Every spring, I plan a backpacking trip specifically to explore a new site in the American West. Those trips have led me to some of the most interesting and beautiful places I’ve ever been. I know others share this interest, too. However, well-known sites like Mesa Verde National Park and Chaco Culture National Historical Park are easily accessible and tend to get crowded. And nothing kills a meditative journey into the past faster than being surrounded by families and sightseers. With that in mind, I compiled this list of hikes to ancient ruins that are off the beaten path. These are real trails that will take you back in time and deep into secluded backcountry. Believe me, I understand the temptation to interact with ancient art when you discover it on a trail. However, nothing could be worse for their conservation. Touching ancient structures, pulling potsherds out of the soil, or handling artifacts can be devastating to these sites. If you are interested enough in these structures to seek them out and hike to them, visit them with respect. Follow local guidelines and rules of the area you’re hiking in. Stay on the trails and always practice Leave No Trace. And while these sites may be part of history, it’s a living history: As one Bears Ears ranger explained to Backpacker, rock art and dwellings are sacred to the Native communities whose ancestors lived there. When you’re visiting, treat them with the same reverence people treat churches, temples, cathedrals, or other religious sites. Salt Creek Canyon is located in the southeastern part of Canyonlands National Park. You can thru-hike the north-south trail in either direction, or do an out-and-back from either trailhead. The canyon is chock-full of fantastic rock formations, natural arches, and Ancestral Puebloan ruins. Along the way, you’ll find granary after granary, where the Ute who lived here stored masa flour and corn. There is a large cliff dwelling on a spur off the main trail that you can hike to, and petroglyphs like “America Man,” and the “Five Faces” that are spectacularly well-preserved. At many of these sites, ancient potsherds litter the ground. Pro tip: Water can be hit or miss in Salt Creek, so most hikers tend to go in early spring. There are also numerous side trails to explore along the way, leading to arches and other ruin sites. Trail length: 22.5 miles (one way) Permit required: Yes; permits are required for camping in Salt Creek and are available on recreation.gov four months before the start of each seasonal block. There is also a $35 park entrance fee. Dogs allowed: No At 2.1 miles, the hike to House on Fire Ruin is short, but you can extend the hike past the ruin and follow the trail up Mule Creek for a longer, 6.4-mile out-and-back. This ruin is iconic. It’s built into a small sandstone alcove, and the rock above looks just like flames ejecting from the ruin’s roof. This is just one of over 100,000 known archeological sites within Bears Ears National Monument. Pro tip: If you want to backpack in the area, the nearby Arch Canyon is a 17.3-mile trail with better camping options. It follows a creek and exposes hikers to natural arches and smaller native cultural heritage sites and ruins. You could hike both trails on the same trip, as the trailheads are less than 5 miles apart, and one permit would work for both areas. Trail length: 2.1 miles out-and-back (to the ruin), or 6.4 miles out-and-back along the Mule Creek Trail Permit required: Yes; $6 reservation fee and $5 per person day-hiking fee Dogs allowed: Yes Just a few miles south of the House on Fire Ruin is another equally spectacular heritage site. Moon House Ruins are perched on a cliff overlooking McCloyd Canyon. One of the buildings has a room with the phases of the moon depicted inside—for all intents and purposes, an Ancestral Puebloan wall calendar. The hike to the structure is mostly moderate, though it involves some scrambling and sections with rope handlines. You’ll be treated to a great view of the ruins from a distance as you approach, so bring those binoculars. After 1.4 miles, you’ll descend into the canyon and cross it to Moon House. To the north and south of the main ruin site, there are other structures to check out as well. Pro tip: Visitors to Moon House Ruins are limited to 20 people per day. Reserve your permit online ahead of time on the recreation.gov Moon House Ruins webpage. Trail length: 4.5 miles out-and-back Permit required: Yes; $6 reservation fee and $5 per person day hiking fee Dogs allowed: No In southern Colorado, the Canyons of the Ancients National Monument is a must-see for anyone interested in the history of the southwest. The Sand Canyon to East Rock Creek Trail to Rock Creek Trail Loop is an 11.8-mile circuit that connects three trails. Along the way, you’ll encounter sandstone caves and views of Marble Mountain, Horseshoe Mountain, Black Mountain, and Ute Peak to the south. It makes for a long day, especially if you plan on stopping to take in the scenery and check out the Puebloan ruins along the way. Not all ruins are marked, so you’ll have to look carefully to find some of them. Dispersed camping is allowed in the Canyons of the Ancient National Monument, but try to find sites that have been used before and minimize your impact. Pro tip: You can hike the Sand Canyon Trail, which goes straight to the ruins and back. However, the loop is actually shorter than the direct out-and-back and has less elevation gain. Trail length: 11.8-mile loop Permit required: No Dogs allowed: Yes This trail starts in the Hovenweep National Monument in Utah and takes you over the border and into Colorado. It’s a 12.4-mile out-and-back that climbs and descends in both directions. The trail offers sweeping views of the monument and passes many unique rock formations. It’s also just north of a designated rare lizard and snake study area on the Colorado side, so keep your eyes open for critters. There are numerous Puebloan ruins along the way, like the “Twin Towers” and “Hovenweep Castle.” Pro tip: Hovenweep National Monument does not allow dispersed camping, but there is a large 31-site campground situated along this trail .3 miles past the trailhead. You can also connect this trail with others on the Colorado side that go into Bureau of Land Management (BLM) land, where dispersed camping options are available. Trail length: 12.4 miles out-and-back Permit required: No; however, there is a $20 entrance fee for Hovenweep National Monument Dogs allowed: Yes This is the one hike on this list that I included even though it requires a guide. Keet Seel is the largest Ancestral Puebloan structure in Arizona, and it is impressive. Unsupervised visits to the site are not allowed. However, the monument does offer seasonal guided overnight trips to Keet Seel in spring (April and May) and fall (September and October). The full out-and-back hike is a long 17.2 miles and can be very strenuous. It descends into a canyon and climbs back out, going both directions. But the reward is worth it. Daily visitors are limited to 20, and guides offer insight into the history of the ruins and the Puebloans who lived there. Pro tip: Plan several months ahead, and check the NPS Keet Seel webpage continually for updates on when you can apply for these trips. Guided overnight tours book up very fast and are only available when there is adequate staff. Trail length: 17.2 miles out-and-back Permit required: Yes; check the NPS Navajo Nation webpage for information on how and when to apply. Dogs allowed: No

item.title: Six things locals wish visitors knew about Hawaii
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 3.13
'Aloha is more than a word we say': Six things locals wish visitors knew about Hawaii From the true significance of a lūʻau to what "aloha" actually asks of you, a native Hawaiian tells you what locals wish every visitor understood before arriving. It's a Saturday morning on O'ahu's North Shore, and as soon as I step onto the beach I see that a crowd has formed around a honu (green sea turtle) basking on the sand. Phones are out. Someone reaches down and touches its shell. A father sets his baby on its back for a photo. "Hey Uncle, no touch da honu!" The words are out of my mouth before I've even finished walking over. The crowd startles – not because they meant any harm, but because I was loud, and none of them had any idea they'd just broken federal law. Get to know your expert Wendy Awai-Dakroub is a Native Hawaiian journalist, entrepreneur and nonprofit leader based in Honolulu, Hawaii. She helps local youth and volunteers with Mālama i Nā Honu, a nonprofit dedicated to protecting Hawaiian green sea turtles. Millions of travellers visit Hawaii each year for its paradisiacal beaches, postcard views and chill vibes, but few look beyond its touristy surface to understand how we Native Hawaiians actually live. Hawaiian culture is deeply rooted in aloha – treating people with care and respect – and aloha ʻāina, our love and responsibility for the land that sustains us. That meaning shapes how locals greet each other, and how we live with the land. Bring that awareness with you, and you'll get it back in full. From respecting our natural landscapes to the right way to eat poke, here are things Hawaiians wish visitors knew about Hawaii before coming. 1. Our native animals deserve space Hawaiian green sea turtles and Hawaiian monk seals rest directly on Hawaii public beaches in plain sight. Getting close to one feels like a rare, magical moment, which is why so many visitors react excitedly when they see one. But the best thing you can do for them is to stay back. Photograph from a distance and treat a resting turtle or seal the way you'd treat a sleeping stranger on a park bench: worth noticing, not worth approaching. Both species are protected under federal and state law, so respecting their space isn't just polite – it's how you actually get to keep admiring them. 2. Our gatherings aren't spectacles A commercial lūʻau in Waikīkī is a popular way for visitors to learn about Hawaiian celebratory traditions. But the lūʻau many of us grow up with don't come with an audience. They are family celebrations, where extended families come together to eat, dance and enjoy music. The name comes from a dish made with young taro leaves that was traditionally served at these gatherings. Today, a lūʻau might mark a birthday, graduation, wedding or other milestone. Preparation can take days, with family coming together to cook and set up for a full day of celebrating. It often feels like a family reunion, with multiple generations around the same table "talking story": a Hawaii Pidgin expression for sitting together, catching up, and sharing stories, usually with pupus (snacks). The honoree is often covered in lei and gifts. If you're invited to a local lūʻau, it's something special, the difference between seeing something and being welcomed inside. Don't expect a schedule or a show – just join in. 3. Aloha doesn't mean no boundaries "Aloha" is one of the most recognised Hawaiian words, but "hello" and "goodbye" are just a fragment of its meaning. The way locals use it, aloha is about truly acknowledging others and treating people and places with care. Aloha is also a two-way street: you can be welcomed warmly and still be expected to understand when something isn't yours to enter, take, photograph or experience. Visitors sometimes roam beaches or rural areas assuming the land is open, picking coconuts, fruit or flowers without realising they've entered someone's property. Some of Hawaii's most photographed places, including Mauna Kea and Kīlauea Volcano are also wahi pana (sacred places). Take photos respectfully, stay on marked paths, don't enter restricted areas, and never take or move natural or cultural objects. Learning a place's significance before visiting helps you understand its boundaries. Aloha is more than a word we say – it's our way of life. 4. 'Where are you from?' is an invitation, not small talk Elsewhere, this question can feel like filler. In Hawaii, it's often one of the first things you're asked. Some visitors find it intrusive, but it isn't meant that way. It's how we get our bearings with someone new: Where are you from? Who's your family? Do we know anyone in common? We ask everyone, not just visitors, even people who have lived here for years. And once the conversation opens up, it usually keeps going. Respond with more than just your city, and real doors can start opening. One conversation can turn into an invitation to a lūʻau. It's part of how we get to know you and decide how far to bring you in. That sense of connection also shows up in how we address one another. You'll hear "auntie" and "uncle" everywhere in Hawaii, even between people who aren't related. They're familiar terms of respect, especially for someone older than you, but they also reflect something deeper: in Hawaii, you don't always have to be family to be treated like family. 5. The shaka is more than a photo pose In Hawaii, the shaka – a loose fist with both thumb and pinky pointing out – is its own language. We use it to greet someone across a parking lot or to show aloha or respect, all without saying a word. On the road, we let each other merge in and out of traffic all the time, and the expected "thank you" is a wave or a shaka out the window. Honking is frowned upon and is only for real emergencies, not impatience. Practice the shaka before you arrive so it feels natural when you need it. 6. 'Hawaiian' food is different than 'local' food Ask most visitors what "Hawaiian food" is, and they'll describe what they ate on their trip. But much of what they're describing is actually "local" food – dishes from the many cultures and communities that now live in Hawaii. "Hawaiian" food refers specifically to the traditional cuisine eaten by the Indigenous people of the islands. More like this: Today's local cuisine reflects Japanese, Filipino, Portuguese and Chinese influences from the plantation days – think plate lunch, malasadas and Spam musubi. Traditional Hawaiian foods like poi, kālua pig (whole pig roasted in an underground oven) and laulau (meat and salted fish steamed in taro leaves) have deep Indigenous roots, but Hawaiian restaurants are few, so many visitors may never taste them unless they know where to look. Poke is a clear example of how the Hawaiian way of eating fish has evolved into something very different. The original includes fresh local fish, sea salt and limu kohu (a native seaweed). No rice, no bowl, no sauces. The "poke bowl" came later, inspired by Japanese chirashi (sashimi over sushi rice). Poke simply means "to cut crosswise into pieces" in Hawaiian. Today's poke bowls, loaded with sauces and toppings, are far from poke as locals know it. A poke bowl isn't meant to be piled high with mix-ins – the fish is the point, so less is more. For poke the way locals eat it, head to a neighbourhood grocery store, where it's sold by the pound at the seafood counter. --

item.title: The 4,554m hike to Europe's highest overnight stay
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 2.45
Rifugio Capanna Regina Margherita: An icy 4,554m hike to Europe's highest overnight stay You can sleep over at this historic mountain refuge straddling the Italy-Switzerland border – but only if you're willing to undertake a days-long, high-altitude icy mountain trek. I'm roped to four strangers, concentrating on the light cast by my headtorch, as I wend my way through the icy labyrinth of crevasses tearing across the Alpine Lys Glacier. We've been here since 05:00, tugging each other ever higher up the Monte Rosa mountain massif towards the highest altitude building in Europe. We've just reached a giant mountain bowl filled with clouds of snow. The milky blue twilight fades to the soft glow of dawn. Our guide squints into the distance. "Up on that ridge" he says, "Do you see it? That's the Margherita refuge." I can't see anything, but the peak he's pointing towards is so sheer sided that I'm convinced he must be mistaken. We press on and, by midday finally arrive at the summit, 4,554m (14,941ft) above sea level. The crystal frosted world of the Punta Gnifetti peak is revealed. I can see the refuge now. I gasp. Somewhat resembling a giant tin can, the narrow three-storey metal building is not so much built onto the mountain as it is balanced on the edge of a precipice. On one side is a steeply falling snow slope and on the other, there's just a vertical kilometre of thin air. A refuge fit for a queen Sharing the Alpine border between Italy and Switzerland, the Monte Rosa massif contains some of the highest peaks in the Alps, including Monte Rosa itself, which at 4,634m (15,203ft) is behind only Mont Blanc. Punta Gnifetti (also called Signalkuppe) comes in sixth. It's here where an Italian scientific research facility and mountaineers' shelter was constructed and named for the then-queen of Italy, Margherita of Savoy. The queen, famed for her adventurous, athletic nature, insisted on climbing to the refuge herself for its 1893 inauguration and spending the night. Plan your trip: When to go: The Rifugio Capanna Regina Margherita is staffed only between mid-June and early September. This is a very popular hike, so make guided tour, accommodation and travel reservations well in advance. The refuge sleeps 70 in summertime. How to do it: Most people climb with a qualified local guide on organised tours, which depart daily in summer. To stay overnight at the rifugio, choose the three-day climb. What you need: Winter clothing, sturdy mountain hiking boots and crampons (not micro spikes). More than a century later, the refuge still supports scientific research while also operating as a mountain hut (rifugio) offering rustic accommodation and thrilling panoramic views. Hiking the massif's eternal winter landscapes has become a popular trek in its own right. Roughly 30,000 hikers summit the peak each year and 4,000 stay overnight, ready like me – and Queen Margherita – to say they've slept in the continent's highest beds. I opted for a three-day guided hike, which requires crampons and ropes. As a frequent hiker, this didn't faze me. If anything worried me, it was the altitude. The hike to the refuge involves a dramatic gain in altitude, from 1,200 to 4,554m (3937 to 14,941ft) in just two days, so steady acclimatisation is essential. More than 4,000m into the air My journey began a day earlier in the Italian mountain village of Alagna Valsesia, at the slopes of the Monte Rosa massif – the literal end of the paved road before the mountainous ascent. From here, a series of cable-car rides whizzed me uphill to Punta Indren, (3,275m/ 10,745ft) where I met my guide and the four other members of our climbing group. Since we were all still acclimatising, our first day involved little more than an hour's hiking across rock and ice to where we would spend our first night, the Rifugio Città di Mantova (3,498m/ 11,476ft), a large wooden mountain refuge set just below the start of the Lys Glacier. There was a marked difference in temperature from Alagna Valsesia, but by wrapping up warm from the biting wind, I could enjoy the panoramic terrace with views of the green valley far below. Despite the stunning setting, I slept fitfully – due, I suspect, to excitement about the coming day's 1,000m (3,281ft) ascent and my body adjusting to the altitude. It was almost a relief when the alarm went off at 04:00 and we crawled out of our beds. We strapped the crampons onto our boots to prevent sliding on the glacial ice and roped ourselves up together – just in case someone slipped into a crevasse. We set out over the glacier and, after an hour or so of hauling ourselves through a spiderweb of crevasses, cleared a ridge and trudged across the mountain bowl. Behind us, dawn clouds bubbled in the valleys and ahead stood the walls of 4,000m (13,123ft) peaks. Despite the drama of the Alpine scenery, this middle section of the hike was considerably easier than traversing the steep, ruptured and torn up glacier crossing. Before I knew it, we were starting the final haul up to the refuge. Although I've never suffered major ill effects from altitude, I do struggle with vertigo. As we zig-zagged sharply up the summit cone, teetering alongside a ridge that fell away into the haze, I began feeling the unmistakable dizzy sensation kicking in and, instead of taking in the view, concentrated on where I was placing my feet. But when I next raised my head, we had made it. The vertigo eased as I stepped out onto the snowy dome. Fold after fold of mountain peaks sparkling with icy crowns stretched out around me – and the refuge itself. I was exhausted. But would I be able to sleep in what was easily one of the most hair-raising buildings I had ever seen? The highest sleep in Europe Once inside, the refuge felt more like a safe cocoon, and it was easy to forget how precarious our situation was. A dining room took up almost the entirety of the ground floor while the upper two were filled with dormitory-style beds which, the night of my stay, were completely booked. I dropped my backpack onto one of the bunks and headed downstairs to order a frothy bowl of cioccolato caldo (hot chocolate) topped with a dollop of Chantilly cream. As I savoured the drink, I fell into conversation with Tommaso Bagnati, one of the refuge's four wardens, who told me how the weather conditions can bring the reality of living on the top of Europe into stark focus. "When there's a big storm the building shakes a bit and you can feel very small," he said. "If there's a thunderstorm it can feel like you're right in the middle of it. All our supplies are delivered by helicopter, so when the weather is very bad and the helicopters can't fly, you can feel a bit cut off from the world." As I sat down to dinner, a weather front rolled across the mountains. The refuge became blanketed in clouds and sleet splattered against the windows. Sitting next to me at the communal dining table was Chinese YouTuber Jianpeng Cui, who told me that despite the "end of the world" feel to the place, he was pleasantly surprised. "I thought there'd only be a bed," he said. "No toilet. No kitchen. But it's not at all like that. I can even buy pizza and juice up here!" I was relieved that altitude sickness had missed me this time. But not everyone was so lucky. Mikhail Morozov, whom I met on his way down from the summit, had suffered headaches and nausea. "Coping with the altitude was the hardest part," he said. "I wasn't acclimatised and you go up very fast. After a couple of hours, the altitude started to hit me hard." More like this: Life in the Rifugio Capanna Regina Margherita – as with all mountain huts – is very communal. Sleeping at high altitude in a cramped dormitory with seven or eight strangers, sharing two toilets with no shower, means you get far cosier than you perhaps want. But the shared effort of reaching the refuge also creates an easy camaraderie. "The best part for me has been meeting people from all over the world who have come here to climb the mountain," said Craig Shaw, a New Zealander living in Switzerland. "Seeing all these different nationalities together in this refuge is just phenomenal". Perhaps the real magic of this mountain is not just its ability to support a crazily positioned refuge. It's an ability to bring people together. --

item.title: Why visitors to Prague should drink in a 'hospoda'
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 2.32
Why visitors to Prague should drink in a traditional pub Prague is synonymous with pubs – but for the real thing, travellers should venture away from its touristy centre and seek out an old-school "hospoda". My wife and I were sipping beers at a pub in Prague's Žižkov district when the bartender plopped two foamy pints of pilsner in front of us. We hadn't ordered them. We weren't even finished with the ones we were drinking. "Oh, we're in one of these pubs" I said, quickly covering my pint with a cardboard coaster. "When you've had enough, just do this." Most visitors to Prague are likely to linger in its Old Town Square, marvelling at its Gothic and Baroque splendour. They'll zigzag through the narrow cobblestone streets to the 14th-Century Charles Bridge and then trudge up to Prague Castle. Everyone should do this on a visit to Prague. But if you only explore its tourist-mobbed centre, as many people do, you'll miss out on one of the most quintessentially Czech cultural experiences: whiling away a few hours in a real Czech pub, where the beer only stops coming if you know the code. A city synonymous with beer It's no secret that Czechs love beer. After all, they drink nearly 150 litres of it per capita every year, making the Czech Republic the top beer-consuming nation in the world. Prague itself boasts the most pubs per person of anywhere on the planet. Your local expert David Farley is a food and travel writer who lived in Prague for three years and regularly writes articles for the BBC, The New York Times, The Guardian and other publications. He has probably spent a year or two of his life in Czech pubs. But just as most New Yorkers don't dine in Times Square and most Londoners don't eat in Piccadilly Circus, you'll rarely find Praguers drinking in Old Town, where bars cater largely to outsiders. Instead, to really get under the skin of Czech culture, you should venture to one of Prague's most atmospheric areas: Žižkov (pronounced Zheezh-kof), a gritty, working-class neighbourhood that has long had a proud reputation for its salt-of-the-earth pubs, and where the bartender's job is to make sure your glass is never empty. Home to hilly cobblestone streets and graffiti-tagged 19th-Century blocks of flats, Žižkov is home to classic pubs such as U Vystřelenýho Oka and U Slovanské Lípy. Despite its relative proximity to the centre of town – tram number 9 will get you there in about 20 minutes – you won't find a lot of guidebook-clutching tourists wandering around. "If you want to understand Czech pub culture, it's hard to find a better place than Žižkov," said Martin Havlin, co-founder of Prague Craft Beer Tours and a born-and-bred Žižkov denizen. "The big difference is that pubs in Žižkov are still mainly for locals. Nobody is trying too hard to look 'authentically Czech' for tourists. You'll find people having a beer after work, old guys at the same table they've probably occupied for 30 years, and a tapster who already knows what half the room is drinking." Žižkov's traditional Czech pubs, called hospoda, are one of the few places where people from all walks of Czech society mix naturally. Hospoda etiquette • If you you're sitting at a table, you're expected to wait for the server to take your order. Unless it's clearly indicated otherwise, don't order at the bar yourself. • Glasses are served wet at a hospoda, so always take the beer mat. It goes under your beer and will save you a wet table – and probably a few looks from the staff. • In Czech lager, foam is part of the beer, not something stealing space in the mug, so don't send it back because you think the glass hasn't been filled to the line. It has. "You can have a construction worker, lawyer, university professor and pensioner sitting at neighbouring tables drinking exactly the same beer," said Jakub Neužil, Havlin's colleague at Prague Craft Beer Tours. "Most importantly, though, they would understand that going to the pub in Czech culture isn't necessarily about 'going out drinking'. Historically, the hospoda has been an extension of the living room: somewhere to meet friends, discuss football, politics, work and life. Beer happens to be at the centre of it." These "living rooms" are great places for travellers to meet English-speaking regulars. A simple "how long have you been coming here?" may soon lead to stories about how hospoda have played an instrumental role in Czech history. Prague was the capital of the Kingdom of Bohemia, and until World War Two, German was widely spoken here alongside Czech. By the latter half of the 19th Century, Czech speakers had begun separating themselves from the German population, and the Czech National Revival, which would eventually result in the creation of Czechoslovakia in 1919, was fomented in Czech cafes and pubs. "At the time, pubs played an important role as gathering places for revivalists, patriots, politicians, writers, artists et cetera; they became centres of associational and cultural life and were one of the few places where Czech was commonly spoken," said Dr Jiří Vinopal, a Senior Fellow at the Institute of Sociology at the Czech Academy of Sciences in Prague. During the heavily oppressive socialist period from 1948 to 1989, Vinopal explains that Czech pubs were "used more as an environment for escape". More like this: Today, pubs are as much a part of Czech life as ever – and a big draw for tourists – but it's increasingly harder to find the kind of old-fashioned hospoda where historical conversations flow as easily as the beer. The city's modern offerings tend to be cleaner and smoke free, with classic fried cheese sharing menu space with dishes like pumpkin soup and cauliflower pancakes. How to drink at a real Czech pub? Havlin's advice is to simply find a busy pub in Žižkov, sit down, order a beer and don't rush. "Watch how people behave, how the beer is poured, order some Czech pub food and maybe start a conversation – and definitely don't leave after one beer." He adds, "That’s the beauty of a real [hospoda]. You're not being shown Czech culture – you're just sitting in the middle of it. And after the second or third beer, you might even start feeling like a local." While sipping your beer and meeting regulars, you may also notice the way Czech bartenders treat Czech beer differently than the more touristy pubs in Prague's historical centre. It starts with the bartender taking a chilled mug and re-rinsing it using a counter-top spray device to ensure there's no fat residue. Then they use the Czech-invented Lukr side-tap to pour the beer, ensuring there's at least three fingers' worth of foam; the side-tap allows the bartender more control of the foam and emits far less gas into the drink than the traditional top pull, making the beer from the Lukr side tap less likely to bloat the stomach. "This developed because beer has been such an important part of Czech culture," said Lucie Janečkova, co-founder of Institut PIVO, a Prague-based school providing beer-focused bartender training. "We've learned that brewing a good beer is only half of the job. What happens to it between the brewery and the guest can completely change the final experience." There is a common saying among Czech bartenders: 'The brewer brews the beer; the bartender makes it.'" There's also an etiquette to drinking once your beer arrives. "When you get a beautifully poured beer, drink it while it's fresh – don't leave it sitting on the table for half an hour," added Janečkova. "And if you're drinking with others, clink glasses with your first beer and say 'cheers' in Czech – 'na zdraví!'" She adds, "And perhaps the most Czech rule of all: if someone says, 'Let's go for one beer,' you probably shouldn't make any plans for the rest of the evening." And, as my wife learned, if you're in a pub in Žižkov, even the bartender won't let you go until you finally put that beer mat atop your empty mug. --

item.title: The controversial US art of engraving whale teeth
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 2.11
Scrimshaw: The controversial art form on the brink of extinction As Moby Dick turns 175, some of the last American scrimshanders grapple with the legacy of maintaining one of the US's oldest art forms. Jade Gotauco spent her childhood among the skeletons of giants. Her father, Chet Gotauco, was a scrimshander – an artist who etched images onto the ivory of hunted whales. In pensive moments, she would slip under the arched jaw of a whale in his Rhode Island garden and sit atop a massive vertebra, watching insects scrabble across the porous bone. "My favourite smell in the world is the sandy aroma of ivory dust," said Gotauco, now an artist herself. Whale teeth adorn the walls of her studio in New Bedford, Massachusetts; she engraves them with nautical scenes in which sperm whales thrash the ocean to foam and whalers hurl barbed harpoons from minute boats. Ask Americans about the cultural legacy of whaling, and many will point to Herman Melville's classic novel Moby Dick, which turns 175 next month. Yet for all the book's brilliance, it's scrimshaw – the practice of artistically carving whale teeth and bones, which is considered one of the US's earliest homegrown art forms – that offers a true insider's view of the industry. Today, there's hardly any of those teeth and bones left on the legal market. Some scrimshanders, including Gotauco, believe the art form should disappear with them. "When the ivory is gone, this is over," she said. Scrimshaw was developed by sailors whose lives unfolded on whaling grounds around the globe as the industry expanded into a 19th-Century behemoth. They strove to depict a culture that, for a few lucrative decades, made New Bedford North America's wealthiest city per capita. "They saw their experiences as important," said Marina Wells, an assistant curator at the New Bedford Whaling Museum, which is home to the largest scrimshaw collection is the world. "You see that in their commemoration of whaling scenes, in all their meticulous detail." Some of the carvings throb with yearning, depicting homey scenes of faraway families. Others capture sailors rowing fragile, open boats dwarfed by the whales they pursued. They're communicating "the dangerous, faraway world of whaling", Wells said. "You have the bloody spouts of the whales after their lungs have been punctured… the intimacy of whalemen interacting with whale bodies that's really hands-on." To modern eyes, the scenes evoke the heartbreaking impacts on species hunted to the brink of extinction; yet the whalers, too, were often broken by the industry. At the Seamen's Bethel, an 1832 mariner's church located across the street from the museum in New Bedford (and which features in the opening chapters of Moby Dick), such risks are on poignant display. Lining its whitewashed sanctuary are marble cenotaphs commemorating those lost at sea. "After fastning to a whale, was carried overboard by a line and drowned," reads the tomb of Captain William Swain. Three sailors from the whaleship Cowper, aged 19, 22 and 24, share another memorial: "All lost by the upsetting of their boat, July 15, 1854, in the Ochotsk Sea." They died as American whaling reached a short-lived fever pitch. In 1857, more than 10,000 men worked aboard New Bedford whaleships, half the city's population at the time. Two years later, petroleum was discovered in Pennsylvania and the ensuing oil rush flooded American cities with kerosene – a comparatively cheap fossil fuel that would eclipse the whale oil used in lamps around the globe. By the turn of the century, American whaling was all but over. Scrimshaw lived on, however. The massive scale of the whaling industry produced a glut of teeth and bones, a byproduct that, at the time, had little commercial value. They gathered dust in attics and warehouses. "When I was a kid they had barrels of whale teeth down at the wharves and sold them for a couple of bucks apiece," recalled Michael Vienneau, a scrimshander on the nearby island of Nantucket, Massachusetts – another onetime whaling hub. Former homes of whaleboat captains surround his small shop, Scrimshander Gallery, in the heart of the island's historic district. A few blocks away is the Nantucket Whaling Museum, whose own significant scrimshaw collection includes pieces by Nantucket whalemen – and famed scrimshanders – Frederick Myrick and Edward Burdett. In the 1960s, scrimshawing surged in popularity, part of a folk-craft revival. (It even got a boost from US President John F Kennedy, an avid collector.) That's when Vienneau got his start, rummaging for cheap whale teeth as a teenager while visiting the island with his family. "Back then, everyone was a scrimshander," he said. "Now I'm one of the last." In part, that's because of the 1973 Endangered Species Act, which tightly restricted the sale of marine ivory. Today, scrimshanders engraving whale teeth and bones must work from the dwindling supply of teeth and bones that remain from before the act was passed – Vienneau has a stash in the back of his shop. "You'll pay several thousand dollars for a raw tooth now," said Vienneau. On a recent afternoon, he was sitting at his workstation squinting at a sperm whale tooth he was engraving with a scene of a sailor brandishing a harpoon at the tail of a diving whale. More teeth were piled in a nearby filing cabinet. His dog, Petey, grabbed a tooth and began to chew on it. Vienneau laughed. "Any dog that gnaws on a sperm whale tooth is a scrimshander's dog," he said, not getting up. As whale teeth grew scarce and expensive, some scrimshanders innovated, carving on cow bones and deer antlers. Even comparatively tooth-rich Vienneau experimented. Once, he flew to Alaska on a tip and spent three days digging a 30,000-year-old mammoth tusk out of permafrost near a remote copper mine. Yet, many purists insist that while such projects are both art and craft, they are not true scrimshaw, since the authentic form relies on the byproducts of historical whaling. Gotauco is one of them. Like some of her peers, she believes this means that scrimshaw is on the brink of extinction. Gotauco works exclusively on pre-1973 ivory and bones. Nearly a century ago, her grandmother emigrated to Boston from Newfoundland, and among her few belongings was a collection of whale teeth and bones she'd inherited from her family of seal hunters, cod fishermen and whalers. That's what Gotauco carves in her New Bedford studio, etching images onto the physical remains of her ancestors' legacy. Along with the whale teeth, Gotauco's grandmother passed along stories of what she said were Mi'kmaq roots. Whales factor into traditional Mi'kmaq stories, and the First Nations community hunted the animals sustainably long before the arrival of Europeans in North America. With her own deep reverence for whales, Gotauco has, at times, felt deeply uneasy about working with ivory. In the years since she learned how to carve scrimshaw by sitting beside her father in his workshop, Gotauco often wondered about the ethics of using materials pulled from the sea with such violence. Commercial whaling was an environmental disaster and a cruelly dangerous job; the beauty of the art form it spurred still catches at her heart. In the end, she embraced it as a form of remembering, calling it "the best way to honour the whales and whalers", albeit one that will likely fade in her lifetime. "When I run out of teeth along with everyone else, I'll raise a cup to the story's end," she said. "May we never get more." --

item.title: Tteokbokki (Spicy Korean Rice Cakes)
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 5.06
Saucy, spicy tteokbokki stars tteok (chewy Korean rice cakes). Stir-frying the rice cakes gives them lightly crisp edges before they simmer in an umami-rich anchovy-kelp dashi spiked with gochujang and gochugaru. A generous amount of onion brings sweetness to balance the chile heat. Bok choy isn’t traditional, but its crisp-tender texture is a welcome counterpoint to all that chew. Odeng (Korean fish cakes) adds another bouncy texture, though you can leave it out. Hard-boiled eggs round things out and are particularly good dragged through the spicy sauce. Tteokbokki FAQs What kind of rice cakes should I use for tteokbokki? Look for cylindrical Korean rice cakes, sometimes labeled tteok or tteokbokki tteok. This recipe calls for the approximately 2½"-long variety, cut in half on a diagonal. Look for them in the freezer section at Korean and other East Asian grocery stores. Or online at sites like Weee! How spicy is this tteokbokki? This version is quite spicy, with heat from both gochujang and gochugaru. If you’re sensitive to spice, you can omit the gochugaru (Korean chile flakes), as some readers have done successfully. Keep in mind that the heat level of gochujang (fermented chile paste) varies by brand. What makes tteokbokki sweet? Tteokbokki recipes often balance their chile heat with sweetness. While some versions use sugar or rice syrup, this recipe relies on a generous amount of cooked onion to sweeten the sauce. Do I need fish cakes to make tteokbokki? No. Korean fish cakes, or odeng, are a common addition and bring a pleasantly bouncy texture, but they’re optional here. The anchovy-kelp broth provides plenty of savory depth without them. Recipe information - Total Time 45 minutes - Yield 6 servings Ingredients ¼ 3 1 8 8 ⅔ 2 1 ¼ 1 1 2 3 2 Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Bring ¼ small onion, thinly sliced, 3 medium-large dried anchovies, one 2x2" piece dried kombu, 2 garlic cloves, smashed, and 3½ cups water to a boil in a small pot or large saucepan. Reduce heat to medium-low and simmer at least 15 minutes and up to 45 minutes (the longer the stock simmers, the more flavor it will have). Step 2Strain stock through a fine-mesh sieve into a heatproof measuring glass; discard solids. Return stock to pot and reheat over medium. Add 8 oz. assorted frozen odeng (Korean fish cakes), bring to a simmer, and cook until just heated through, about 5 minutes. Step 3Meanwhile, mix together ⅔ cup gochujang (Korean hot pepper paste), 2 Tbsp. soy sauce, and 1 Tbsp. gochugaru (coarse Korean red pepper powder) in a small bowl. Step 4Heat ¼ cup vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. cylindrical Korean rice cakes (about 2½" long), cut in half crosswise on a diagonal, and cook, turning occasionally, until crisp, about 5 minutes. Add remaining 2 large onions, thinly sliced, and remaining 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced; cook, stirring, until softened, about 2 minutes. Add gochujang mixture and cook, stirring occasionally, until combined and fragrant, about 1 minute more. Step 5Add fish cakes and 2½ cups stock to rice cake mixture and stir to combine. Bring to a boil, then reduce heat to low and simmer, stirring occasionally, until sauce is thickened and rice cakes are tender, about 5 minutes. Step 6Add 1 medium head of bok choy, stems cut into ¼" pieces, leaves cut into 1" pieces, and 1 scallion, thinly sliced on a diagonal, and toss to combine, adding more stock by the tablespoon to thin if needed. Cook, tossing occasionally, until bok choy is wilted, about 2 minutes. Step 7Transfer tteokbokki to a platter. Top with 3 large eggs, hard-boiled, halved lengthwise, 2 Tbsp. toasted sesame seeds, crushed, and remaining 1 scallion, thinly sliced on a diagonal. item.title: Onigiri (Japanese Rice Balls)
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 4.58
Stuffed with savory fillings and wrapped in crisp nori, Japanese rice balls called onigiri are made for eating on the go. A convenience-store staple in Japan, they’re just as handy tucked into a lunch box or picnic basket. The key to onigiri that hold their shape is properly cooked Japanese short-grain rice. Rinsing and soaking the rice helps it cook evenly; shaping it while still slightly warm helps the grains stick together. Use damp, salted hands to prevent sticking—no rice cooker or onigiri mold required. This version offers three fillings: creamy tuna mayo, tart and salty umeboshi (pickled plums), or spicy kimchi. Once you’ve got the technique down, feel free to experiment with cooked salmon, spicy tuna, cod roe, leftover chicken salad, or crab meat. Just avoid anything too wet, which can make the rice balls difficult to shape. Onigiri FAQs What kind of rice is best for onigiri? Japanese short-grain rice, often labeled sushi rice at US supermarkets, is the best choice. When cooked, the grains cling together enough for the onigiri to hold their shape. Long-grain rice, such as jasmine or basmati, won’t hold together as well. How do you keep onigiri from falling apart? Shape the onigiri while the rice is still warm, using firm but gentle pressure to pack the grains together. Keep the remaining rice covered as you work so it doesn’t cool or dry out, and wet your hands with the salted water in the recipe to prevent sticking. What can you put inside onigiri? This recipe offers options including tuna mayo, umeboshi, and kimchi, but cooked salmon, spicy tuna, cod roe, leftover chicken salad, or crab meat are all fair game. Whatever you choose, avoid excessively wet fillings, which can make the onigiri harder to shape. Can you make onigiri ahead of time? Yes. These onigiri can be made up to two days ahead. Wrap each one tightly and refrigerate. For crisp nori, leave it off until you’re ready to eat; otherwise it will soften as it absorbs moisture from the rice. Recipe information - Total Time 1 hour 10 minutes (plus soaking) - Yield Makes 12–16 Ingredients 2 3 1 2 1 4 ⅓ ¾ ¼ Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Place 2 cups sushi rice in a large bowl and pour in cold water to cover by 2"–3". Gently swish around with your hands to rinse, then drain. Repeat process until water is almost clear (about 3 more times). Pour cold water over rice to cover by 1" and let soak 30 minutes (this will help the grains cook more evenly). Drain well in a fine-mesh sieve. Step 2Combine rice and 2½ cups water in a medium saucepan and bring to a boil, stirring occasionally. Reduce heat to low, cover, and simmer until water is absorbed, 12–14 minutes. Remove from heat and let rice sit (still covered) 15 minutes. This will allow rice to steam and become tender. Uncover and gently fluff rice with a fork. Let sit until cool enough to handle but still warm. Step 3Meanwhile, cut three 8½x7½" toasted nori sheets into 3x1¼" strips with kitchen shears; set aside. Step 4Prepare the fillings. Mix one 5-oz. can tuna, drained, 2 Tbsp. mayonnaise, and 1 tsp. soy sauce in a small bowl to combine. Place 4 umeboshi (Japanese pickled plums) on a cutting board. Working 1 at a time, press a chef’s knife against fruit until pit is exposed; pull out and discard. Set fruit aside (no need to chop). Working over the sink and using your hands, squeeze liquid out of ⅓ cup Napa cabbage kimchi; chop into small pieces. Step 5Place 1 cup water in a small bowl and stir in ¾ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Dip your hands into salted water, then scoop a little less than ⅓ cup rice into 1 hand. Form into a thick disk 3"–4" in diameter (keep remaining rice in pot covered). Create a small indentation in the center and add 1–2 tsp. tuna mixture or kimchi or a whole umeboshi. Mold rice up and over filling to create a sphere (filling should not be visible), then press firmly with index finger and thumb to form into a triangle. Place on cutting board or a baking sheet. Repeat with remaining rice and fillings, dipping your hands in salt water each time. (You’ll have extra tuna—save it for making a tuna salad sandwich or spooning onto crackers.) Step 6Place ¼ cup furikake or toasted sesame seeds on a small plate. Wrap bottom of each onigiri with a strip of reserved nori, then roll remaining exposed sides of onigiri in furikake. Do Ahead: Onigiri can be made 2 days ahead. Wrap tightly and chill. Editor’s note: This onigiri recipe was first published in September 2020. item.title: Sweet and Tangy Collard Greens
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 3.68
Collard greens have deep roots in Southern cooking. They’re a fixture on New Year’s Day, when eating greens is said to bring prosperity in the year ahead. Chef Julia Sullivan of Henrietta Red in Nashville serves them alongside black-eyed peas every January 1. “It’s something my mom has always done, and I think my grandparents, too,” she says. “It’s a superstitious thing.” Sullivan’s collard greens get their savory, subtly smoky flavor from bacon, onion, garlic, and red pepper flakes. They simmer until silky-tender in just under an hour, then get a sweet-tart finish from apple cider vinegar and a little sugar. This recipe intentionally leans tangy. If you like your collard greens less acidic, start with 2 Tbsp. vinegar instead of the full ¼ cup, then add more to taste. Collard greens FAQs How do you clean and prep collard greens? Remove the tough center ribs and stems. Next, stack the leaves, roll them up, and slice them crosswise into 1"-thick strips. Dunk the prepped collard greens into a large bowl (or sink!) filled with water. Swish the leaves around to loosen the grit and let them sit for a few minutes. Remove the greens from their container (don’t pour them out or the grit will get back on the leaves) and shake to remove excess liquid. There is no need to dry the collard greens for this recipe; a little bit of water helps them steam and wilt down. Why do you add vinegar to collard greens? Vinegar balances collard greens’ earthy, slightly bitter flavor and cuts through the richness of the bacon and broth. Adding it near the end of cooking keeps its flavor bright. This recipe calls for ¼ cup apple cider vinegar, but you can start with half that amount and adjust to taste. Can I make these collard greens without bacon? Yes. The bacon is optional, so you can simply leave it out, or trade it for beef or turkey bacon. For vegetarian collard greens, also swap the chicken broth for water or vegetable broth and add savory depth with a spoonful of miso paste. What other types of greens work with this recipe? Any sturdy cooking greens can work here, but expect differences in flavor and cooking time. Mustard greens and turnip greens are equally beloved in the South; either will make a slightly sharper, more peppery batch of greens. Kale is also a fine alternative. More delicate Swiss chard will become tender much faster, so reduce the cooking time accordingly. Recipe information - Total Time 55 minutes - Yield 8 servings Ingredients 3 4 1 4 1 3 3 ¼ 2 Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Heat 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium. Add 4 oz. slab bacon, finely chopped, if using, and cook, stirring occasionally, until some fat begins to collect in pot and bacon starts to look shiny, about 5 minutes. Add 1 medium onion, finely chopped, and cook, stirring occasionally, until golden and softened, 5–7 minutes. Add 4 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and 1 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 30 seconds. Step 2Add 3 lb. collard greens (about 3 bunches), ribs and stems removed, leaves sliced crosswise 1" thick, to pot a large handful at a time, letting greens wilt slightly after each addition before adding more. Add 3 cups low-sodium chicken broth or water, bring to a simmer, and cook, stirring often, until greens are wilted and have lost about half of their volume, about 4 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low, partially cover pot, and simmer gently, stirring occasionally, until greens are tender and liquid is almost completely evaporated, 25–30 minutes. Step 3Stir ¼ cup apple cider vinegar and 2 tsp. sugar into collard greens and cook until sugar dissolves, about 1 minute; season with kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper. item.title: Cottage Cheese Lasagna
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 3.68
Cottage cheese lasagna skeptics, hear us out. Unlike ricotta, which can turn chalky, small-curd, whole-milk cottage cheese stays moist through the long bake. And when mixed with nutty Parmesan, melty Fontina, eggs, and garlic, it makes an exceptionally creamy lasagna filling. A combination of ground beef and hot Italian sausage brings plenty of flavor and richness to the meat sauce, while tomato paste and Worcestershire sauce give canned tomatoes long-simmered depth without the long simmer. Keep the sauce loose: That extra moisture is what cooks the regular dried lasagna noodles right in the baking dish. (Yep, no boiling required.) This may not be nonna’s classic (we’ve got BA’s Best Lasagna for that), but it’s deeply savory, exceptionally cheesy, and considerably easier to assemble. Cottage cheese lasagna FAQs What kind of cottage cheese should I use? Whole-milk cottage cheese is nonnegotiable. Lighter versions can make the lasagna watery and less flavorful. We prefer small-curd for texture, but large-curd works just fine if that’s what you have. Read more about our staff favorite cottage cheese brand: Do you have to boil lasagna noodles before baking? Regular dried lasagna noodles go directly into the baking dish—no boiling or soaking required. The relatively loose tomato sauce provides enough moisture to cook the noodles until al dente as the lasagna bakes. Can I make cottage cheese lasagna ahead of time? Yes. The baked lasagna can be refrigerated for up to 2 days. Let it cool completely, cover loosely with foil, and reheat, covered, in a 325° oven for 30–45 minutes, or until warmed through. You can also make the meat sauce up to 2 days ahead and refrigerate it in an airtight container; there’s no need to reheat it before assembling the lasagna, but you may need to add a few minutes to the baking time. You can also freeze the assembled, unbaked lasagna for up to 2 months. Thaw in the refrigerator overnight and then bake as directed. Can I use ground turkey? Absolutely. Swap the ground beef for ground dark meat turkey and the pork sausage for Italian-style turkey sausage. Because poultry is leaner, add an extra drizzle of olive oil if the pan looks dry. Recipe information - Total Time 2 hours (plus sitting time) - Yield 8–12 servings Ingredients 1 1 8 2 8 3 2 1 1 ¼ 1 2 6 12 2 24 12 Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 1 lb. ground beef (20% fat) and 8 oz. hot Italian sausage, casings removed, breaking up into small pieces with a wooden spoon, until well browned and cooked through, 10–12 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer meat to a medium bowl, leaving fat behind. Step 2Add 2 large onions, finely chopped, 6 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt to same pot; if pot looks dry, add up to 1 Tbsp. more oil. Cook, stirring often, until onions are translucent and golden around the edges, 8–10 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. double-concentrated tomato paste and 1 Tbsp. dried oregano; cook, stirring constantly, until paste is brick red and beginning to stick to bottom of pot, 5–8 minutes. Return meat to pot. Step 3Add one 28-oz. can plus one 14.5-oz. can crushed tomatoes, ¼ cup Worcestershire sauce, 1 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper to pot. Bring to a simmer, stirring occasionally and scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pot. Remove from heat and stir in 2 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about 1 cup). Taste tomato sauce and season with more salt if needed. Step 4Toss 12 oz. Fontina cheese, grated (about 3 cups), and remaining 4 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about 2 cups), in a large bowl to combine; measure out 1 cup cheese and set aside for topping. Add 2 large eggs, 24 oz. whole-milk cottage cheese, and remaining 2 garlic cloves, finely chopped, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper to remaining cheese in bowl. Mix vigorously with a wooden spoon until combined. Step 5Arrange 3 regular dried lasagna noodles in a single layer in a 13x9" baking dish. (If noodles are long, arrange parallel to long sides of baking dish; if noodles are short, arrange parallel to short sides of baking dish. Don’t worry about any gaps—noodles will swell as they cook.) Spread 1½ cups tomato sauce over noodles. Scatter one third of Fontina mixture evenly over sauce (mixture will be stiff; use hands to break off small pieces and scatter over sauce). Starting with another layer of noodles, repeat process, creating 4 layers of noodles in total and ending with a layer of tomato sauce. Top lasagna with reserved cheese. Step 6Place baking dish on a large rimmed baking sheet (to catch drips) and bake lasagna until sauce is bubbling around the edges, top is golden brown, and noodles are al dente (insert a skewer into center of lasagna to check), 75–85 minutes. Let sit at least 15 minutes and up to 45 minutes before serving. Do Ahead: Lasagna can be baked 2 days ahead. Let cool completely; cover loosely with foil and chill. Reheat, covered, in a 325° oven until warmed through, 30–45 minutes. Editor’s note: This cottage cheese lasagna recipe was first printed in September 2023. It has been updated for style.
