item.title: The Great Date Boom is Here
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 2.92
There's nothing the internet loves more than a trendy ingredient. A few years ago, tinned fish became the It girl of the proverbial pantry, inspiring folks to swap their cheese boards for brinier, braver "seacuteries." Then cottage cheese blew up. Creators on TikTok and Reels proved that the creamy breakfast staple could be whipped, baked, blended, braised, and even frozen and churned for a delicious, protein-packed snack. Now, in 2026, we've seemingly reached peak pickle, with pickle-flavored everything from lip balms to (yes, even) lube. But the newest snack darling is one of the oldest ingredients in the world: the date. We saw it firsthand during Pantry Awards judging, when date-based products started landing in our submissions pile in numbers we hadn't seen before. These fiber-filled fruits are having a moment, in new and unexpected ways. Sour date snacks, date-sweetened boxed cakes, date-based candies and syrups, even the world's first soft drink made from dates—the primordial fruit is being reimagined for modern times, and people love it. "Consumers are starting to see dates as more than just a traditional dried fruit," says Amanda Sains-Harris, vice president of marketing for the date-based snack brand Joolies. Sains-Harris explains that the date boom has been a long time coming: Dates have been gaining popularity on social media and at industry trade shows for years. Now the fruits are flying off shelves. The category is up 24.1 percent in conventional grocery channels through June 2026, she says, citing point-of-sale data from the market-intelligence platform SPINS. As with cottage-cheese ice cream and tinned-fish cheese boards, folks seem to be looking for a healthy snack that still tastes good. Cardboard protein bars and chemical-tasting sodas are a thing of the past. "[Dates] check a lot of boxes without feeling overly engineered," Sains-Harris says. "Consumers also don't necessarily want to choose between better-for-you and indulgent anymore. They want both. Dates naturally live in that sweet spot." Grace Finerman founded Date Smarter!, which makes decadent chocolate-covered date caramels (and won one of our 2026 Pantry Awards, BTW). She agrees that consumers are seeking out healthier alternatives to sugary snacks—but they don't want zero-sugar, either. "Five years ago people were really turning to stevia," Finerman says. "I think the pendulum has kind of switched to people now wanting not cane sugar, but something sweet that's not processed." Despite their sticky sweetness, she says, dates are naturally low-glycemic. They're also high in fiber (6.7 to 8 grams per 100 grams), which is a tempting proposition in the age of GLP-1s and fiber-maxxing. And they make great fuel, especially when filled with protein-packed nut butters. "We actually have a large customer base of endurance athletes, professional and collegiate athletes, and overall fitness enthusiasts," says Sophia Karbowski, co-founder of Realsy, which specializes in date snacks stuffed with different nut butters. "The natural combination of carbs, sugar, and fiber in dates—plus a bit of added protein and fat from the natural nut butter filling—is the perfect source of clean energy athletes are looking for." Dates are also incredibly versatile, which makes them attractive to brands, too. On their own, the dried fruits are indulgent. But wrap 'em in bacon or stuff 'em with something sweet, and they're practically heaven. Since they're so sticky, they make excellent binders. Mashed together à la the viral peanut butter date bark that's taken over TikTok, or blended into a paste, they hold nuts, fruits, and other ingredients together. And when they're dried and powdered, they make an excellent refined-sugar substitute in baking mixes, syrups, and more. "We [Date Smarter!] use date powder, which is when you take a date that's dehydrated and run it through a processor," says Finerman. "We make all our caramel with that." Food trends come and go, but these brands are all betting that dates are here to stay (and given that they've been around since literally Mesopotamia, we think so, too). Karbowski expects to see dates on labels across the whole grocery store, from beverages to baking mixes. Sains-Harris wants to push the boundaries of where the fruits can go, and she's already getting creative: In May 2026, Joolies launched Date Sours, which swap the traditional buttery fillings for flavors like sour blue raspberry and cherry cola. "We always say dates are 'the original palm tree candy,'" says Sains-Harris. "And I think they're finally getting the spotlight they deserve." Whatever happens, we're here for it.

item.title: Everything is a Luxury Item Now
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 2.14
Welcome to Open Tab, a weekly roundup of the news, gossip, and stories that have stayed open in my tabs all week. Last time we covered the rise of AI-made reservations. We must address one oft-ignored issue that’s become too acute to overlook: Whoever is in charge of wine at Trader Joe’s needs a wellness check. I’m seeing apple pie wine. I’m seeing pumpkin spice chardonnay. I’m concerned and I want to help. This week chef Daniel Humm of Eleven Madison Park fame entered the consumer packaged goods (CPG) game. His new product is called Riff, a line of boxed pasta dishes that come with seasoning mixes and crunchy toppings, plus suggestions on each box for how you can incorporate fresh ingredients. (Riffs—get it?) Also important: 13,000 cases later, the CDC has announced the Cyclospora outbreak is over. Phew! One less concern among the many other food safety issues currently unfolding—like “small stones and other hard objects” in ice cream. Also in this week’s Open Tab: why every food item seems like it’s a luxury item, Chipotle’s shiny new partnership with Palantir, China’s blueberry scam, and the legacy of Prince’s favorite cheesecake. The era of expensive everything A burger at DC’s Le Diplomate will set you back $29—more than twice what it cost 13 years ago, as The Washington Post reports. In New York, Gigi’s set off a wave of menu pricing discourse with a $77 roast chicken, they’re doing $100 hot dogs in Florida, and across the country, prices at McDonald’s have doubled over the last decade—even as serving sizes have gotten smaller. Why is everything so much more expensive now? The answer is multifaceted: The war in Iran is skyrocketing fuel prices which, in turn, has a profound impact on global food systems, plus inflation is rising steeply—hence this week’s Fed rate bump—and, finally, restaurants’ supply, labor, and utility costs are still rising. A lot of restaurant items are priced as luxuries, but our sense of luxury has also skewed in recent years. Caviar, once rarified, is now par for the course. Wagyu beef, a high-end, hard-to-source import years ago, is on countless menus at all price points. For $158—that’s two roast chickens at Gigi’s—you can indulge in an all-you-can-eat Wagyu and seafood experience, in fact. All this means diners will learn to be more discerning. With prices like these, determining which meals warrant this kind of spending is all the more important. Why is Chipotle working with Palantir? What’s the opposite of a joint slay? Whatever that term might be, that’s how I’d describe an international fast-casual restaurant chain partnering with a multibillion dollar tech giant hell-bent on destroying every last scrap of data privacy for normal people. I am talking, as you may have guessed, about the new collab between Chipotle and Palantir. Palantir, which has been contracted to work with ICE to track migrants’ movements, will be working with Chipotle on a food safety risk platform—essentially a means to try to reduce the number of food safety incidents at the chain’s locations. “The platform brings key information together in one place, enabling our teams to more effectively identify trends, prioritize follow-up, and make proactive, data-informed decisions,” Laurie Schalow, Chipotle’s chief corporate affairs and food safety officer, in a statement to Wired. Will all of this actually result in greater food safety at Chipotle or is this simply a scheme to collect data on your burrito order? Well, reader, at this juncture it’s hard to say. Approximately a decade and a half ago, the fruit giant Driscoll entered the Chinese market to make blueberries happen, bringing in growing technology to lay claim to the best blueberries with the best genetics, according to The Wall Street Journal. By 2025, Chinese production of blueberries doubled that of the US. But Driscoll wasn’t the only one cashing in on the blueberry rush. Chinese business owners allegedly copied those blueberry-growing technologies, and some even stole Driscoll’s copyrighted blueberry varieties. The blueberry market in China is booming, but Driscoll has filed more than 20 lawsuits (and won two) seeking damages against Chinese companies, according to WSJ’s report. Vanessa Drews started making cheesecakes just for the love of the game—a cheesecake-head, if you will. That all changed when Prince (yes, that Prince) developed a taste for Drews’s desserts. Last September, she opened up a brick-and-mortar shop four miles from the late icon’s Paisley Park home, where she serves up the same Prince-approved recipes. Read on to discover the rest of Drews’s story.

item.title: Prince's Favorite Cheesecake Delivers the Funk
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 2.13
About 20 miles southwest of downtown Minneapolis, in the small town of Excelsior, a curiously named business sits wedged in a strip mall among a taqueria, a nail salon, and a pet groomer. Wander inside and you might think you’re in a museum dedicated to Prince, the Minneapolis-born musical genius who lived just four miles south of here at his private home and recording studio complex, Paisley Park. The purple walls are dotted with photos of the homegrown superstar, who passed away 10 years ago this year. The business may double as a de facto homage to the self-proclaimed Purple Yoda, but it’s actually one of the hottest bakeries in the Midwest. Welcome to Cheesecake Funk. When owner Vanessa Drews opened the cheesecake bakery in September 2025, it quickly became the talk of the baked good loving Twin Cities. And the Prince connection goes far beyond the bakery’s purple walls. But for lovers of all things sweet and creamy, Cheesecake Funk is today a veritable mecca for those in the know. Dig, if you will, the superlative turtle cheesecake laden with rich dark chocolate, gooey caramel, and crunchy toasted pecans, with a crispy bottom crust. The exact recipe for that crust is a secret, but Drews admits to using cinnamon and a healthy portion of brown butter. It’s a masterpiece of contrasting textures and layered flavors, which perhaps explains why it’s Cheesecake Funk’s best seller. For Drews, a single Black mother of two, it all started back in 2002 when she was still a hobby baker. A lifelong lover of cheesecakes, she baked them for family and friends who began requesting them for every party and holiday gathering. “I started tweaking the recipe over time, mixing the crust with brown butter, adding cinnamon here and there,” Drews says. At the time she was working a day job as a senior paralegal and making cheesecake in her free time. But money was tight, and she picked up a part-time gig selling merchandise at Paisley Park on the occasional evenings that Prince threw open-to-the-public parties. One day in 2013, she showed up with a cheesecake. “Prince always had band members and other employees coming here from other parts of the country and the world,” Drews recalls. “So, I put the cheesecake in the fridge with a note saying that anyone was welcome to a piece. I wanted to provide some good food for them and say: ‘Welcome to Minnesota.’” Stocking the fridge with cheesecake became a ritual. Soon Drews noticed the speed with which her cheesecakes were devoured. Who could be responsible? And then, scrolling through the social media site formerly known as Twitter, a particular post caught her attention: A meme of two monkeys trying to resuscitate a fellow simian that featured the words, “The moment you find out somebody ate the last piece of Vanessa’s cheesecake.” It was uploaded from an account managed by Prince. “I thought: ‘Oh my God, I’m the Vanessa he’s referring to!’” she says. “I was euphoric." Prince began calling her edible handiwork “cheesecake funk,” often including the phrase on invitations to parties at Paisley Park, writing “HELPYOSELFTOSOMECHEESECAKEFUNK.” After that, at Paisley Park parties, Prince would occasionally walk by Drews and, with his trademark smirk, say, “What’s for dessert, Vanessa?” before walking away. (This anecdote may surprise Prince fans—there’s a common misconception that he was 100% vegan. Not so, at least when it came to cheesecake.) While Prince’s endorsement certainly boosted her confidence, she didn’t feel ready to quit her job and become a full-time baker. But then, a big break: In 2019, a friend of a friend offered a bite of Drews’s cheesecake to Kam Talebi, founder and CEO of Kaskaid Hospitality, the Twin Cities–based enterprise with 18 restaurants nationwide. He loved it enough to put it on the dessert menu of the Eden Prairie location of Crave American Kitchen & Sushi Bar, a small chain of restaurants scattered across the Midwest. “A few months later, Kam called me and he said, ‘You’d better prepare for volume. I’m adding your cheesecake to all eight Twin Cities locations of Crave,’” Drews recounts. “I remember sitting at my desk at the law office and thinking, Oh my gosh! Is this really happening?” She decided to pull the proverbial trigger. Drews dipped into some of her 401(k) plan to buy baking equipment and set up shop in a rented hotel kitchen. Fast-forward to September 2025, when she opened a bakery near her home in Excelsior, using the moniker Prince came up with, Cheesecake Funk. Prince’s favorite variety, turtle, is decidedly bold, but there are no wallflowers among the 17-plus flavors on offer at any given time, many of them seasonal. This past summer’s flavor, lingonberry, was appropriately Minnesotan given the state’s large population of people with Scandinavian heritage, and it was enough of a hit that Drews added it to the permanent menu. “It’s very tart, but has bursts of sweetness, similar to strawberry,” Drews says. “It’s just really refreshing and light, perfect for summer.” As the weather shifts, it’s on to the next: The current fall seasonal flavors include a deceptively simple apple cheesecake topped with stewed fruit laced with cinnamon. These days, one has ample options when seeking Cheesecake Funk products in the Twin Cities. In downtown Minneapolis, stop by Union Rooftop, Brit’s Pub, Butcher’s Table, Wood + Paddle, or one of a handful of locations of Crave in and around the Twin Cities, or even Paisley Park. Or you can go to the original Cheesecake Funk in Excelsior and say hello to Drews. Prince fans have begun stopping there on their way to or from Paisley Park. “The other day I had a couple from Germany, and this afternoon, these sweet ladies came in from the Netherlands,” Drews says. “People come to find me because they appreciate Prince.” “I’m so thankful to him,” she continues. “Prince is like the gift that keeps on giving.”

item.title: The Most Remote Places on Earth You Can Actually Visit
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 5.24
Reaching the most remote places on Earth takes more than just a plane ticket—it takes patience, endurance, and often a string of connections that make the arrival feel like an achievement in itself. These are places where airports are rare, ships arrive only a handful of times a year, and the communities you meet are outnumbered by wildlife. What they offer in return is a kind of distance that feels almost impossible in the modern world—skies free of light pollution, landscapes shaped by extremes, and the rare quiet that comes from being far beyond the usual travel circuit. Why do we seek remoteness? Journeys to places like these are rarely simple, but that difficulty is part of the allure. They remind us what travel feels like when the destination is hard-won, when the act of arriving carries its own reward. In the Kerguelen Islands, there are no hotels or tour buses, only wind, sea, and wildlife. In Russia's Oymyakon, for example, just stepping outside is an act of endurance. And on South Georgia, hundreds of thousands of penguins gather on beaches once scarred by whaling. In a world where so much feels accessible, true remoteness has become rare. These are the most remote places on Earth that shift our sense of scale and remind us that there are still corners of this planet where distance is intact. Kerguelen Islands, Southern Indian Ocean Nicknamed the “Desolation Islands,” this French territory sits marooned in the southern Indian Ocean, approximately 1,865 miles from Madagascar. Few places feel so utterly cut off. Volcanic cliffs plunge into storm-lashed seas, while king penguins and elephant seals crowd the beaches in their thousands. Nobody lives here permanently—only rotating teams of scientists, engineers, and unconventional travelers. What surrounds you is a world sculpted by wind, sea, and stone, where humanity has left little mark. How to get there: The French supply vessel Marion Dufresne II sails from Réunion Island several times a year. The voyage takes around six days. Quttinirpaaq National Park, Canada On the northern tip of Ellesmere Island, just shy of 500 miles from the North Pole, Quttinirpaaq lives up to its Inuktitut name: “top of the world.” It is a place of extremes—glaciers stretch for miles, jagged peaks rise from polar deserts, and the summer sun never sets. Muskoxen graze the tundra, Arctic wolves hunt in silence, and traces of ancient Inuit encampments remind you how long people have endured at this latitude. Few visitors make it here, but those who do find a landscape that feels infinite. How to get there: Travel first to Resolute Bay in Nunavut, then connect by charter plane to Tanquary Fiord, open only in the summer months. Ittoqqortoormiit, Greenland Few places capture the human will to survive like Ittoqqortoormiit, a settlement of around 450 people perched at the edge of Scoresby Sound, the world's largest fjord system. Wooden houses painted red, blue, and yellow dot the snowy cliffs, while rhythms of life here still follow the seasons: hunting and fishing sustain families, sled dogs line the streets, and in winter the sea ice seals the town off from the outside world completely. The surrounding waters carry drifting icebergs, and it's not unusual to see polar bears wandering the coast. How to get there: Reachable by helicopter from Nerlerit Inaat Airport, itself connected by small aircraft from Reykjavik, Iceland. Longyearbyen, Norway Longyearbyen, in the Svalbard archipelago, is the northernmost town of its size in the world. Despite its isolation, it's surprisingly lived-in, with cafés, a craft brewery, and even a fine-dining restaurant. Beyond town, reindeer roam freely, glaciers carve the landscape, and the Global Seed Vault safeguards the world's crops in a frozen hillside. Here, summers pass in endless daylight; winters in an unbroken stretch of night. How to get there: Daily flights connect Oslo and Tromsø to Svalbard Airport, making it one of the more accessible remote places. South Georgia, South Atlantic Ocean A remote island once known for whaling, South Georgia is now a sanctuary where wildlife has reclaimed the land. More than half a million king penguins gather on its beaches, while elephant seals occupy the shore in extraordinary numbers. Rusting relics of abandoned whaling stations remain, and the grave of polar explorer Ernest Shackleton—the Anglo-Irish Antarctic explorer who led three British expeditions to the Antarctic—lies at Grytviken, a pilgrimage for history enthusiasts. After decades of ecological strain, including the introduction of reindeer by whalers, conservation projects are now restoring the island’s native habitats and protecting its fragile ecosystem. How to get there: No airports exist—visitors arrive by expedition ship, usually as part of cruises departing from Ushuaia, Argentina. McMurdo Station, Antarctica On Ross Island, McMurdo Station is the largest research base on the continent, supporting around 1,000 people each summer. It has been the launch point for many of Antarctica’s most important expeditions, from early 20th-century journeys led by Scott and Shackleton to modern scientific studies on climate change and glaciology. The surrounding landscape—glaciers, volcanic peaks, and the vast Ross Ice Shelf—has shaped much of what we know about the polar world. Travelers can’t stay at McMurdo, but expedition cruises to the Ross Sea sometimes include landings nearby, offering the rare chance to stand at the centre of Antarctic exploration. How to get there: Expedition cruises to the Ross Sea depart from New Zealand or Australia, with limited charter flights from Christchurch supporting specialist itineraries. Pitcairn Islands, South Pacific Ocean Home to just under 50 people, the Pitcairn Islands are one of the world’s least populated territories. Settled by the HMS Bounty mutineers in 1790, the community is still made up of their descendants. Life moves at a slow rhythm, shaped by the island’s rugged volcanic terrain and the surrounding Pacific waters. For visitors, the appeal lies in the intimacy: hiking to hidden caves, diving into crystalline waters, and being welcomed by almost every resident. How to get there: Fly to Tahiti, then on to Mangareva in French Polynesia. From there, a supply ship makes the 32-hour crossing to Pitcairn several times a year. Changthang, Ladakh, India High on the Tibetan Plateau, Changthang is a high-altitude desert where the air is thin and the landscape seems endless. Nomadic Changpa herders graze yak and goats across sweeping plains, while saltwater lakes like Tso Moriri and Pangong Tso shimmer beneath snow-capped peaks. Black-necked cranes, wild asses, and even snow leopards are spotted here, adding to its sense of undisturbed isolation. How to get there: Flights run from Delhi to Leh, followed by an overland journey across rugged mountain passes into the plateau. This article was originally published in Condé Nast Traveller Middle East.

item.title: How I Travel: Shania Twain Brings Spinach To Her Hotel Rooms
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.49
Most people’s carry-on bags hold items like a sweater, book, tablet, chargers, snacks, maybe hand sanitizer, and an eye mask. Pop music icon Shania Twain is bringing a mini recording studio everywhere she goes. “In my carry-on for many, many years is my Pro Tools set-up for recording,” says Twain. “I do a lot of writing and recording in my hotel rooms, so I bring an Apollo [audio-processing hardware], my microphone, the laptop, all of that.” Her latest album, Little Miss Twain, features songs that she wrote and produced years ago, with themes stretching back to her teen romances. The best-selling country-pop artist of all time, Twain got nostalgic with Condé Nast Traveler about her first business-class flight, which she took after signing her record deal, as well as more recent travel—like her 12-night stint performing with Harry Styles in London at Wembley Stadium this past summer—and shared future trips, like the one she’s plotting to India this winter. Plus, other quirky items on her packing list. Her favorite mode of transportation: If we're speaking about touring, bus is my favorite way to travel. I just love moving into it and then not having to unpack every day. I don't love living out of a suitcase. I like to settle in; that's my thing. I like sleeping in small spaces. Her first flight in business class: It was from Toronto to Nashville, after I signed to my record label. They bought me a business-class ticket. People were still smoking on planes then, and I’m so sensitive to cigarette smoke. I thought ‘gee, if you’re moving up in the world, do you have the right to say, Do you mind?’ I was so perplexed that people could smoke in business class, but that was the way it was. And I remember the food was better. Her packing approach: I'm a good packer, a really good packer. I would say I'm a thoughtful packer, in the sense that I've got a good routine down. I pack in categories: I’ll do the shoes, then jewelry, then pajamas, then underwear and socks. Quite organized. How she passed the time in London between shows this summer: I love London. I love to walk, and London has a lot of really quaint, walkable areas with pubs and cafes and shopping. I love Hyde Park. I've ridden horses and gone to concerts there, and it's all walkable from the hotels. And there's the theaters! This summer, I took advantage of seeing Paddington, which was extraordinary. It was just adorable. The cast is really exceptional. I mean, the story is great—we all know the story—but I just thought the theater was ideal for the intimacy of it. Her favorite places to stop through on tour: Quebec City is a great place for a day off on tour. It’s very Paris-like, this little time capsule—like a little bit of Paris was brought over to Canada. It's so quaint and beautiful, and on the water. Very walkable as well. The part of Canada she wants more tourists to see: I would recommend people visiting Canada see more of where I'm from [in northeastern Ontario], because nature is the most extraordinary. We've got areas where you can go moose watching, for example. You're not in a zoo. You see all these wild animals and it's really beautiful. Her priorities when planning a vacation: Food definitely motivates me when I'm traveling. I need to make sure that I'm going to enjoy the food because, as a vegetarian especially, it can be quite limiting. One of my favorite places to visit and eat as a vacation trip is Egypt, because it gives me everything I need. I like to walk everywhere and see the architecture. That's a big thing for me—to see history on every block. I love ancient history particularly, and the cities and villages that are museums in themselves. And then, like I said, the food. The Lebanese food [in Egypt] is extraordinary for vegetarians. So that's a part of the world that I really love. Why she chose to have a home in Switzerland: I had a language base of French growing up in a bilingual town in Ontario and I wanted to maintain that, which I get to do in Switzerland, living on the French side. Plus, the benefit of being in Switzerland is you have the valley and the lakes below, but then you can just drive up for 20 minutes and be on a glacier. I'll never give up my four seasons—and being Canadian, I love winter. The items she needs in her hotel room: One thing I miss the most when I'm traveling in hotels is not being able to cook. I love to cook so I always make sure that there is a really good blender, and that I have things like raw spinach, avocados, tomatoes, and bread—things that I can put olive oil and salt and pepper on and make my own snack without calling room service. The place she’s never been that she’d like to see next: Even though I’ve been very lucky to travel in my career, there's a lot of places I haven't been. I've never been to India. I've got a trip planned this January to Hyderabad, because I have friends from there. I've heard so much about [the country], and I know so many people that have gone, but this will be my first experience. And don't forget, India has the best vegetarian food!

item.title: These US Airlines Have Mishandled the Most Bags in 2026, According to New Data
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.16
Most travelers have experienced that sinking feeling at baggage claim when the carousel stops and their checked luggage is still nowhere to be seen. While lost or delayed bags are sometimes just an unfortunate part of air travel, there are some airlines that statistically mishandle checked bags more often than others. The situation can be extra frustrating in 2026, as most carriers have significantly raised the cost of checking luggage on domestic and short-haul international routes to an average of $45 for the first bag. Despite the elevated fee, US airlines have collectively mishandled 1,120,760 checked bags in the first six months of 2026, according to new data from the Department of Transportation (DOT). That’s an average of about 0.5 bags mishandled per 100 bags enplaned. Although those numbers can seem shocking, they’re similar to mishandled baggage rates for the same stretch in 2025, which saw an average of 0.52 bags mishandled for every 100 loaded into planes’ cargo holds. If you’d like to avoid your carefully packed luggage being on the wrong side of those statistics, it’s a good idea to know which airlines routinely have the highest rates of mishandled bags. The DOT’s monthly air travel consumer reports compare the 13 largest US airlines and how many bags each carrier mishandles per 100 loaded onto planes. A mishandled bag includes baggage that is lost, delayed, damaged, or stolen. In the first half of 2026, American Airlines had the highest rate of mishandled bags, with an average rate of 0.73 mishandled bags per 100 enplaned, the DOT data shows. Closely following is American’s wholly owned regional subsidiary Envoy Air, which mishandled an average of 0.72 bags per 100 enplaned. United Airlines was next, with a mishandled baggage rate of 0.66 bags per 100 enplaned from January to June 2026. On the flip side, low-cost carrier Allegiant Air had the best baggage handling rate, with just 0.12 bags mishandled per 100 enplaned. Travelers who want to keep close tabs on their checked luggage can put devices like Apple Air Tags into their bags and track them during each stage of the flight. Many airlines now integrate Air Tag data into their baggage tracking process, allowing travelers to share the device location with customer service representatives through their mobile apps. item.title: The Best Beaches in Italy, From Sicily to Puglia
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.92
You’d be hard-pressed to find a more quintessential Italian pastime than spending a summer day at the beach—and the best beaches in Italy lend themselves to precisely that kind of leisurely indulgence. The country has nearly 5,000 miles of coastline, so you can bet there’s a piece of waterfront for everyone. Some are long, wide strips of sand dotted by neat rows of lounge chairs and umbrellas, while others are rocky inlets or hidden coves reachable only by boat or hike. The list below culls our picks for the best beaches all along the peninsula and on the islands, from Liguria in the north to Sicily in the south, along with tips on where to stay near each. Some are accessible by train or public ferry, while others require a car (road trip, anyone?). Keep in mind that summer (especially July and August) is the high season, so expect beaches to be more crowded than at other times of the year. For fewer crowds, consider shoulder season months like May, early June, and September. Tips for visiting the best beaches in Italy For some expert advice on planning a beach-oriented itinerary in Italy, we tapped Georgia Yuill, a Condé Nast Traveler Top Travel Specialist and Butterfield & Robinson’s region director for Italy. Though the best time to visit Italy can vary depending on the type of trip you want to have, a beach vacation warrants some summer vibes—and strategy. “The best time to go to the beaches of Italy are on the weekdays of June, early July, and September,” Yuill says. “Waterfronts in Sardinia and Sicily are particularly lovely in September with the water warmed up over the previous months and visitor numbers low, leaving you with a tranquil and gorgeous setting.” Yuill says the beaches can get crowded on the weekends in June, July, and August, when you’re competing not only with fellow tourists for spots on the sand but also with Italians who are on their own vacations as well. “That said, experiencing the coastline or islands such as Sardinia by gulet or catamaran is an excellent solution to finding quiet inlets and harder-to-reach beaches,” says Yuill. This list features beaches that are free to access, but if you can swing it, private strips of sand at beach clubs are a great option as well. “Not only are they perfect for people-watching, but they provide all the things travelers may not have packed, like umbrellas and lounge chairs,” Yuill says. Plus, families traveling to Italy with kids will especially appreciate the lifeguards on duty. And who can say no to the convenience of showers, changing areas, and eateries? Finally, Yuill suggests choosing an area designated as a Blue Flag Beach, which indicates that it is clean and well cared for from an environmental perspective. item.title: An Art Lover's Guide to the Coastal Michigan City of Saugatuck
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.51
With its thriving arts and culture, rich array of farm experiences, dynamic dining landscape, and long stretches of Lake Michigan soft sand beaches, Saugatuck is Michiganders' scenic Midwest escape with plenty of small-town charm. Together with neighboring towns Douglas and Fennville, the region has become known as the Art Coast, drawing painters, writers, sculptors, and musicians for decades and helping to establish myriad local makers. That ethos has inspired this November’s Art Coast Food & Wine Festival (November 5-7), a three-day celebration of Southwest Michigan’s vibrant food and drink scene. Led by several local chefs (along with a few out-of-towners), the inaugural event will feature talks, demonstrations, and collaboration dinners. It’s just one more reason to plan a trip to the area this fall, when summertime crowds have subsided and autumn colors and flavors are underway. What to do in Saugatuck: Beaches, wineries, and art galleries to know The region’s largest outdoor draw is Oval Beach, recognized as one of the most beautiful beaches in the country. Pack the umbrella and take in the shoreline activities—visitors and locals alike come here for swimming, sunbathing, and rounds of frisbee. A large parking lot is right next to the beach, helping to ensure a smooth transition from vehicle to vacation mode. Taste some wine and enjoy the vineyard views at Modales Wines in Fennville. Owners Jim and Carol Gonzalez opened the winery in 2019 with the mission of making local bottles with sustainable practices and world-class vision. Today, they have been recognized as one of Michigan’s only certified organic wineries, with nearly two dozen bottles on offer. Book a guided tasting to sample through several of them, including favorites like the rose, syrah, and the award-winning Sauvignon Blanc or Gruner Veltliner. Pair it up with any of their onsite snacks (especially the goat’s and cow’s milk cheese spreads from nearby Evergreen Lane Farm & Creamery). Explore the area by water with a Star of Saugatuck cruise, a 90-minute sternwheel ride down the Kalamazoo River and onto Lake Michigan. Enjoy the trip during the daytime, or book a sunset cruise for golden hour photo opps. Near this dock, spot the Saugatuck Chain Ferry, a hand-cranked chain ferry that connects the downtown district to Mount Baldhead Park and Oval Beach (in use since 1838, it is the only remaining chain driven ferry in the country). Discover the area’s rich arts scene with visits to local galleries, including J. Petter, Dune, and Button Gallery. And check the calendar at Saugatuck Center for the Arts for regularly scheduled concerts, author talks, and artist exhibits (including the recent Mother Lake from local artist Bryanna Manning). During warmer months, swing by the parking lot on Fridays for a weekly farmers market. Saugatuck has several wonderful downtown shopping options—visit Brass Anchor for women’s clothing and accessories, Leon Footwear for handcrafted footwear, and The Book Nook for many beach read contenders. Spend some time exploring Lulu Cadieux—housed in a historic bank building, the lifestyle boutique celebrates everyday joys through a culinary learning center and thoughtfully curated retail selection. The shop features items across multiple categories, including home, garden, and beauty, and owner Terry Walker plans frequent trips abroad to procure goods (including vintage apparel and accessories). Guests can learn about different cuisines and techniques with the team’s onsite cooking classes, which take place in a spacious, state-of-the-art kitchen (complete with a beautiful cookbook collection). And those seeking more of the shop’s aesthetic and ethos can stay overnight at The Polo Shed, their private guest house. Located a short distance from the shop, the property sleeps up to 12 and features comforts and charms such as feather chandeliers, a grand piano, a stone fireplace, and a chef’s kitchen. Where to eat and drink in Saugatuck and Douglas Noble Twist Taphouse recently opened in the heart of downtown, bringing with it house-made beer and spirits, local wine, and from-scratch, New Haven-style pizza. An old-world patio with string lighting greets diners, who can start with one of the beers brewed onsite. Pair them up with creative salads or sandwiches (think the PBLT, with pork belly, tomato jam, and arugula), or any of the pizzas (with options like hot honey pepperoni or Michigan mushroom). For decades, locals and visitors have been flocking to Everyday People Café. That popularity is indeed for the food, but also for the restaurant’s other charms—its cozy, lively bar, comfortable dining rooms, and warm, polished hospitality. Menu items span regions and cuisines: roasted salmon with sauce soubise, vadouvan vinaigrette, and pea shoots; miso-sake marinated sea bass with Chinese eggplant and lemon-ginger beurre blanc; pesto pasta with gemelli noodles, teardrop tomatoes, and parmesan. Whatever the creation, the team here excels, wielding a true grasp of balanced, flavorful dishes. House-made desserts like the key lime pie or blueberry crisp (try it a la mode) serve as a rich and comforting finale. Chicago native Melissa Corey moved to Saugatuck and opened Pennyroyal Café and Provisions, where she and her team put forth seasonal, from-scratch dishes celebrating Michigan farms. Book a table for dinner, or visit during daytime hours for billowy blueberry pancakes, hearty breakfast sandwiches, and a popular whitefish melt. Pastries are baked fresh daily and beautifully conceived—a Basque-style cake with a pastry cream center, rotating croissants, and a caprese danish on weekends (a seasonal favorite with marinated tomatoes and herbed chevre). Dine indoors to witness Corey and team at work on the line, or outdoors in the dreamy, lush garden. It is walk-ins only for brunch, so be sure to arrive early—tables here fill up fast (credit the hospitable team and Corey’s impressive titles, including Chopped winner and James Beard Award nominee). Take a 15-minute drive to Fennville for dinner at Salt of the Earth, a local favorite for seasonal, sustainably sourced cooking. Start with the bread board, featuring several house-baked varieties alongside local butter, followed by the pizza. The team features several wood-fired renditions: wild mushroom (with caramelized onions and arugula), short rib (with white cheddar and cream sauce), and vegetable (with zucchini, peppers, and corn). When it’s time for dessert, don’t miss their S’more Cake, complete with a toasted marshmallow, graham cracker crumbs, and milk chocolate pudding. Dining at Bowdie’s Chophouse is at once elegant and unfussy, and a nod to some of the best big city steakhouses around. Settle in with big band swing sounds and a house cocktail, then go big with the steaks—filet mignon, or the bone-in ribeye for two. Accompany it all with a few of the restaurant’s signature sides—sautéed mushrooms, truffle fries, or brussels sprouts and pork belly. Leaving town, stop for a bite at Farmhouse Deli & Pantry, a beloved spot for sandwiches, salads, and baked goods—all made in-house and from scratch with local, seasonal ingredients. Don’t miss the turkey club or BLT, or earlier in the day, the breakfast burrito (with cage free scrambled eggs and local white cheddar). Where to stay in Saugatuck and Douglas, Michigan In business for nearly 20 years, Bella Vita Vacation Rentals has become a trusted resource for Saugatuck-Douglas travelers. The company manages more than 45 boutique rental properties within 10 miles of Saugatuck, many of which are located just footsteps from downtown or the lake. Peruse their range of listings, featuring water views, modern amenities, and pet-friendly options. Those looking for a boutique stay right on the water will find it at Lake Shore Resort. The property makes the most of its idyllic location overlooking Lake Michigan, with kayaks, a private beach, a swimming pool, and firepits for sunset gatherings. A variety of room types are available, and each one includes breakfast and access to other resort amenities, such as bikes and yoga classes. The spacious Cottage is perfect for larger parties—two units can be rented together or separately, and each features two bedrooms, a washer/dryer, walk-in showers, and gas ranges. Keep an eye on their calendar for upcoming events and programming, including occasional collaboration dinners with local partners. What was first built in 1937 as the home of former Saugatuck mayor Frank Wick became The Wickwood Inn in 1981, the town’s first bed-and-breakfast. Originally modeled after London’s Brown’s Hotel, the property recently underwent a redesign by award-winning Soucie Horner Design Collective, resulting in a refined, modern aesthetic. Several luxury suites welcome guests, along with The Bungalow—a three-bedroom retreat with ensuite bathrooms and curated artwork. When you’re not enjoying the comforts of the room, explore the inn’s amenities, including its English gardens, farm-to-table breakfasts, daily social hours, and heated pool.

item.title: 9 Standout Galapagos Cruises for Sailing the Bucket-List Wildlife Destination
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.20
An extraordinary archipelago 600 miles off the coast of Ecuador, the Galapagos promise a once-in-a-lifetime travel experience—and many agree there's no better way to visit, than by ship. Unlike the typical island-hopping cruise itinerary you'll find elsewhere, Galapagos Island cruises invite travelers to experience some of the most unspoiled environments on earth. The vessels here are small, too—sometimes accommodating as few as 16 passengers. There are no water parks, Broadway-style shows, or casinos on board. Instead, pristine surroundings, uninhabited islands, and rare wildlife are the featured attractions. These cruise itineraries offer the chance to get up close to giant tortoises and playful sea lions, to snorkel among coral and stingrays, and look for rare birds like the blue-footed booby, a species only found in parts of the Pacific Ocean. Leave the logistics to your captain, and let yourself enjoy an incredible adventure of hiking through untouched natural environments or kayaking, paddleboarding, or snorkeling through one of the most interesting parts of the Pacific Ocean. After all, in the Galapagos, animals outnumber people and some of the most interesting scenes are found on the water. Cruises to this remote region usually span about a week and visit multiple islands. And while it is generally an expensive destination, given the hard-to-reach nature of the islands, there are some more affordable ways to cross off this bucket-list trip. Below, we cover nine of the best Galapagos cruises—with options for every type of traveler. The best Galapagos cruise for luxury travelers Ecoventura offers one of the most luxurious—and family-friendly—cruises in the Galapagos. The company operates three expedition yachts, Origin, Theory, and Evolve, each of which can accommodate 20 guests across 10 staterooms. Children six and up are welcome on board, and some staterooms can be connected to create spacious family suites. The crew is the shining star of these yachts, ensuring personalized service, pleasant surprises—like a pirate-themed send-off party to end the trip—and a menu to suit every palate. There’s a breakfast buffet every morning featuring Ecuadorian specialties and international favorites, and a multicourse dinner every night, with plenty of options for vegetarians. Onboard Ecoventura’s yachts, kayaks, stand-up paddleboards, snorkeling gear, and zodiacs are on offer. There’s also a hot tub, fitness center, and plenty of outdoor nooks for taking in the unforgettable views. Off the ship, experienced naturalists lead daily excursions to lava fields, scenic viewpoints, idyllic snorkeling spots, and secluded beaches. Even if you're new to watersports like snorkeling, the ship’s patient guides will teach you how to get comfortable in the water so you can enjoy swimming among turtles, fish, and stingrays. The best Galapagos cruise for solo travelers Join a small group of future friends on the Reina Silvia Voyager, G Adventures’ newest catamaran that’s custom-built for sailing the Galapagos. Two of its 10 cabins feature single beds and are reserved for solo travelers. All come with a private bathroom, desk, and a large picture window to frame the pristine Galapagos views beyond. A 10-day itinerary starts and ends in Quito, taking guests on a journey through the Central and East Islands to look for sea lions, iguanas, and a seemingly endless variety of birds. Go kayaking, snorkeling, scuba diving, or paddleboarding—or kick back and relax on the spacious sundeck while enjoying some of the most unspoiled views in the world. There’s a chef on board to ensure you never go hungry, a hot tub to soothe any sore muscles, lots of spaces for socializing when you want to, and a bar that’s perfect for sunset cocktails—with or without your shipmates. The best Galapagos cruise for travelers craving personal space The Celebrity Flora is one of the largest ships sailing the Galapagos Islands, but don’t expect it to be packed with crowds. While it's about twice the size of the Celebrity Xploration, which also sails to the Galapagos, the Flora carries the same number of people—about 100. The size difference gives the ship a more spacious feel and roomier suites that start at around 224 square feet. Some cabins have floor-to-ceiling windows that open up to make your suite feel like it has a balcony. Others have actual balconies, some as large as 321 square feet. These eco-conscious ships are designed to navigate the most remote parts of the Galapagos Islands. There’s also a retractable marina onboard to make it easier for travelers with mobility issues to get in and out of the vessels ferrying them from ship to shore. The best Galapagos catamaran cruise Avalon Waterways may be better known for its European river cruises, but it also sails the Galapagos Islands, with a chartered luxury catamaran, the Treasure of the Galapagos. The boat can accommodate a maximum of 16 guests and offers a rare amenity in the Galapagos: private balconies. The largest suite comes in at 430 square feet and features not one but two private outdoor spaces. Guests feast on dishes from creative, locally inspired menus featuring seasonal ingredients. There’s also a hot tub and a naturalist on board, and fares include wine with dinner as well as coffee, tea, and water. The best Galapagos cruise for foodies There may be few better places to eat in the Galapagos than The Grill, one of two restaurants on board the Silver Origin, a 100-passenger ship operated by the luxury cruise line Silversea. The Grill serves up premium cuts of meat cooked tableside atop fiery lava stones. Indulge in locally sourced lobster, Andean quinoa, and fresh Galapagos-caught fish. Meals at The Grill are served alfresco, and it’s hard to find a better view for dinner than these natural landscapes. Elsewhere onboard, guests can learn the art of ceviche-making from the ship’s chef and sample Ecuadorian cheese that has been aged in lava tubes. The smallest suites on board are 325 square feet, and many come with balconies. Even the showers offer ocean views, and there’s butler service onboard for anything you might need. While the Silver Origin is another one of the largest ships sailing the Galapagos Islands, these voyages tend to sell out—book early. The best Galapagos cruise for adventure seekers Sailings on board the La Pinta, operated by Uncruise, are designed for adventurous spirits who also appreciate time to unwind. This isn’t the newest or most luxurious ship sailing the Galapagos, but it’s comfortable, unpretentious, and recently refurbished. Onboard this 48-passenger yacht, you’ll find plenty of gear: kayaks, paddleboards, snorkeling equipment, scuba equipment, and a glass-bottom boat included. The itinerary includes visits to seven islands and islets as well as a visit to the Charles Darwin Research Station. Hike Dragon Hill on Isla Santa Cruz while looking for iguanas and flamingos, paddleboard alongside sea lions at Isla Floreana, or enjoy a stroll along a secluded white-sand beach. If you think cruising isn’t your thing, Uncruise might just change your mind. The best Galapagos cruise for science lovers If ever you’ve wondered what life would be like as a scientist, HX Expeditions has the Galapagos cruise for you. The company operates a Citizen Science Program on board the MS Santa Cruz II, enlisting guests to help with completing research projects. Guests can join onboard researchers in collecting samples, learn to make field observations, and visit the onboard science lab to analyze materials and work with experts to process data. Between following in the footsteps of Charles Darwin, visiting his namesake research station, and working with onboard researchers, this is a vacation where learning is accessible—and prioritized. The best affordable Galapagos cruise For travelers craving the wild majesty of the Galapagos at a more affordable price, Nature Galapagos & Ecuador delivers an authentic, expertly curated experience that doesn’t compromise on adventure nor break the budget. Specializing in small-ship and land-based tours, their budget-class cruises—aboard intimate, 8 to 10-person yachts like the New Flamingo and Merak—offer access to remote islands, expert bilingual naturalist guides, and daily excursions that bring you face-to-face with marine iguanas and Galapagos tortoises. Accommodations are simple but comfortable, with snorkeling gear, meals, and interisland logistics seamlessly included. Expect to spend around $3,000 for a four‑ to five‑night cruise, compared to about $7,600 for a seven-night sailing on G Adventures. The best Galapagos cruise for kids Inspire your kids to learn about science and exploration by hopping on board the National Geographic Gemini, a ship that sails the Galapagos as part of a partnership between Lindblad Expeditions and National Geographic. These journeys, led by National Geographic experts, give kids the chance to become National Geographic Explorers-In-Training. The exclusive, hands-on program is designed to teach kids about geographical exploration and scientific research. The National Geographic Gemini can accommodate up to 48 passengers in 27 suites. More than a dozen suites come with private balconies, and one of those balconies is large enough to accommodate a private hot tub. But don’t fret if that suite is already booked; there’s a whirlpool hot tub on the sundeck that’s open to all guests. There’s also a library, well-stocked bar, and meals made with locally sourced ingredients on board. FAQ: How early should I book a Galapagos cruise? For the widest selection of vessels and sailing dates, aim to book your cruise four to nine months ahead of your intended sailing. More spontaneous travelers may find last-minute deals booking two to eight weeks ahead of their intended departure, though some itineraries will be sold out by then. Where do I embark on a Galapagos cruise? Getting to the Galapagos requires some logistical planning. After flying into Quito or Guayaquil, passengers typically spend a night in one of these mainland destinations before flying to the islands to board their ships. Your cruise line will tell you where to be on the islands for your departure, and in some cases, flights from the mainland will be included (or booked for an additional fee). When is the best time to cruise the Galapagos Islands? With a consistently mild climate year-round, the Galapagos can be visited at any time, although certain seasons offer exceptional wildlife viewing. December is when the giant tortoises hatch, and July marks the mating season for blue-footed boobies and short-eared owls. In April and May, marine iguanas typically hatch, while sea turtles begin laying their eggs at the start of the year. Given the diverse wildlife and year-round natural phenomena, there's never a "wrong" time to visit the islands. Are Galapagos cruises expensive? The Galapagos Islands aren’t a bargain destination. Expect to pay somewhere between $5,000 and $12,000 per traveler, depending on the ship, itinerary, and length of the voyage, though there are options starting in the $3,000s. What kind of wildlife can I expect to see on a Galapagos cruise? The Galapagos Islands are renowned for their unique wildlife, including giant tortoises, marine iguanas, blue-footed boobies, and sea lions. The islands’ ecosystems are so diverse that you can see a variety of species in different environments, from volcanic shores to lush highlands. item.title: The Best Hotels Near the Sphere in Las Vegas
item.description:

I’ve been taking trips to Las Vegas since long before the Sphere was there, and half the fun—for me, at least—has always been staying somewhere central in this wonderfully over-the-top city. Whether you’re planning around the event of your dreams or simply want to experience Vegas’s newest and most iconic orb in all its glory, these are the hotels worth checking into less than a 10-minute drive from the Sphere. item.title: The Most Comfortable Travel Pants That Aren’t Sweats or Leggings
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.78
When I travel, I want to be comfortable—but not at the cost of looking put together. There’s a time and a place for sweatpants (and yes, we’ve all boarded a flight in them), but I’d argue the best travel pants are something more versatile: soft enough for a six-hour flight, stretchy enough for a spontaneous sprint to the gate, breathable enough for wandering a new city, and spruced up enough to wear straight to dinner. That sweet spot is something many of us editors at Condé Nast Traveler think about—and, frankly, obsess over. The good news is that there are plenty of options beyond your standard jogger. Think jeans with just the right amount of give, yoga pants that pass surprisingly well as trousers, lightweight utility pants with room to roam, and clever, packable styles designed for staying put in your suitcase until you need them again for the flight home. Our editors have tested dozens of travel pants in cities all across the globe—and some really stand out for comfort, versatility, and style. Below, the tried-and-true travel pants we recommend wearing on the plane and long after you land. Dress pants Spanx's Ponte pants feature a high-rise waistband with comfortable, built-in compression, offering a flattering silhouette. Commerce director Madison Flager recommends this pair for work trips, and loves how the wide-leg design balances structure and roominess. Available in petite, regular, and tall inseams, they accommodate a range of heights, enhancing fit and ease. The fabric is stretchy yet firm and resistant to wrinkles, making these pants a functional choice for all kinds of elevated travel outfits. Thanks to their soft, menswear-inspired fabric and a partially elastic waistband, transportation and travel news editor Hannah Towey says this pair of pants from Abercrombie feels “basically like sweatpants.” The pleating details and low-rise, tailored cut flatter curves, while the wide-leg design ensures breathability. The pockets add utility for holding onto travel essentials, and their ability to retain their shape and resist wrinkles makes them suitable for all sorts of run and play. Utility pants The Prana Halle pants are commerce writer Jessica Sulima's go-to for trips that involve anything mildly outdoorsy. According to Sulima, they're great on a hike (and can be rolled up and pinned at the calf once you start to sweat), but are also water-repellant, which makes them a great thing to pack in case of unexpected rain. “I find the low-rise bootcut to be incredibly flattering, which makes me feel better about wearing them on a plane or train,” says Sulima. “Plus, they pack light, compared to more cargo-style hiking pants on the market.” Pull-on pants Made from a viscose and recycled nylon blend, these pants combine structure with stretch, offering a flattering kick flare and pull-on elastic waistband for comfort and ease. Senior features editor Rebecca Misner calls them indestructible: “I think you can basically set them on fire and then still wear them,” she says. Their durability is key for frequent travelers—and despite the elevated price, they’re a reliable investment thanks to the softness, stretch, and structure of the fabric. The tailored silhouette can also be dressed up or down, making the pants ideal for transitioning between travel, work, or play. With soft cotton, an elasticized waist with drawcords, and an easy pull-on structure, this Gap pair could appeal to just about anyone. “These pants are currently working overtime for me as both my go-to flight pants, and maternity pants," says global social director Mercedes Bleth. She's taken them all over the globe—all the way from NYC to Saudi Arabia then Atlanta, on a road trip to Maine, and beyond. And throughout Bleth's pregnancy, she has prioritized buying things that she'll be able to wear long after her bump disappears. “These pants have been, and will continue to be, my go-to when I need of something structured and cute, but also incredibly comfortable,” she says. Global digital director Arati Menon's travel rule is simple: Pick clothes that have room to stretch or settle into (she's notorious for pretzeling her body into a tight economy seat). “Comfort doesn’t have to be at odds with style—I like to play with form and volume, and these balloon pants do just the trick.” According to Menon, who gets plenty of compliments on them in the airport, the pair is perfect with an oversized cotton or poplin shirt (Arket and Dissh are her favorites) and perhaps a more fitted ribbed tank. Flager lived in these linen pants this past summer—and loved them so much that she bought them in both brown and black. “They’re just such a great travel day pant; they're more put together than sweats or joggers, but not at all constrictive,” says Flager. They may be leaving her regular rotation as the weather cools down, but she's already looking forward to pulling them out again for December trips to Jamaica and Florida. Comfortable jeans After years of testing and reviewing travel pants, I can confidently say: Silver Jeans knows how to do denim for the road right. These are one of the newer pairs I love for short flights, days that turn into nights out, and weekend road trips from NYC. You can’t go wrong with its classic light wash color, and the fact that they fold down super thin is such a satisfying win. As a 5'3" girlie, finding jeans that elongate your legs is rare. But when I pair these with a slight platform Chelsea boot? Instant legs for days. I’ve already gotten so many compliments on them. These soft, stretchy jeans from Halara offer high-waist support and a flattering fit without waistband pinching or digging, crucial for extended wear during flights or road trips. Loved and recommended by commerce editor Meaghan Kenny, she says the pants are basically pajamas masked in a dark-wash denim design complete with a stylish cuffed hem. Kenny has worn them extensively without any loss in quality, and mentions that she always receives compliments on them. item.title: Where was 'The Dog Stars' filmed? The surprising mountainous hideout that stood in for Canada's peaks
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.91
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favourite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was The Dog Stars filmed? The year is 2035. Along a mountain range on the south side of Denver, survivors are navigating an unprecedented, post-pandemic world. A deadly flu outbreak has wiped out a vast majority of the human population, and many who have survived remain with a debilitating blood disease. This is the premise of Ridley Scott’s latest blockbuster, starring Jacob Elordi as young pilot Hig, Margaret Qualley as Cima and Josh Brolin as Bangley. While Bangley has no intentions of leaving the efficient homestead he and Hig have settled into, Hig is determined to track down other survivors, frequently embarking on tracking missions alongside his trusty dog, Jasper. As these stories unfold in a post-apocalyptic world far from crumbling metropolises, the natural world plays a major role in Scott’s latest movie. While set in Canada, filming took place in Italy between April and June 2025. “The size and scale of the production footprint in Italy was ideal for what we needed,” says The Dog Stars production designer Chris Seager. “We found a combination of quality locations that could convincingly represent Colorado, while also being relatively close together. This allowed us to work much more efficiently from a production point of view.” “We also considered Canada,” says Chris. “But ultimately Italy offered the best combination of location quality, scale and practical logistics. Being able to concentrate so many of the locations within a manageable area was a huge advantage for the production, helping us maximise our time and resources.” So where exactly did the team set up camp during the epic-scale production? Here, we uncover some of the key locations to keep an eye out for. Cinecittà Studios, Rome While much of The Dog Stars’ cinematography took place beside forests and mountain peaks, Rome’s Cinecittà Studios played a crucial role in the scenes set at Grand Junction Airport. “Cinecittà was amazing,” says Chris. “It quickly became evident that, to achieve the scale and complexity of the effects that Ridley wanted, we needed to work on a soundstage where we could have complete control over the environment.” Chris recalls how the set within Europe’s largest film studio was built in just four weeks. On the studio filming, cinematographer Erik Messerschmidt said, “[Cinecittà Studios] houses Italy’s most modern sound stages. It’s the centre of studio production and is familiar to all local crew. It was the best and most obvious option.” Abruzzo Much filming also took place in Italy’s Abruzzo region. One such apocalyptic scene honed in on the city of Avezzano. Chris says: “One of the biggest and most challenging locations was the petrol station [in Avezzano] where we filmed the city landing sequence – we actually landed the plane in the street! We transformed the location entirely: we trashed the petrol station and the surrounding area to create the sense of a world that had been abandoned and reclaimed by nature. The greens department and the layered set dressing played a huge role in this. “To represent the cycle of life, we created a swimming pool and diving board, which we filled with dead bodies and overgrown vegetation, crocuses growing through the remains. It was a very strong visual expression of the post-apocalyptic, graphic world, but it also presented considerable logistical challenges in terms of access and working within the location.” EUR, Rome The Roman business and residential district of EUR (Esposizione Universale Roma), known for its cultural happenings and Fascist-era architecture, saw the production team set up more post-apocalyptic scenes. “The Roman neighbourhood of EUR stood in for the Denver city hall triage centre where Hig goes to retrieve supplies. It was a challenging place to shoot, as it’s normally a busy city, but the Roman authorities were very helpful in making it happen for us, and it was ultimately one of the most successful sections of the film,” says Erik. Bordano Bordano was an empty field that is used for hang-gliding, so we had to transform the entire site from scratch,” says Chris. “We built nine airplane hangars, Bangley’s house and tower, as well as a number of smaller sheds and a trailer home. We also dressed large quantities of grass and other greenery to make the location feel abandoned and overgrown.” “The whole process took approximately five weeks, which was a very tight turnaround given the scale of the build. The major benefit of working on location was the sheer amount of space and the ability to create the environment at the scale required, rather than being constrained by a studio. It also allowed the buildings, runway and surrounding environment to exist together as one cohesive world, giving the finished locations a greater sense of authenticity and scale.” The Dog Stars is in UK cinemas now
