item.title: This Restaurant Rocks (No, Literally)
item.description:
Source: Eater Score: 4.35
A version of this post originally appeared in Eater Today, which spotlights the freshest news and stories from across the food world every day. Subscribe now. “There’s a rock in the sink!” That was the takeaway last winter after the East Coast contingent of the team that writes this newsletter met for brunch at Flynn McGarry’s stylish, Scandi-inflected Gem Home in lower Manhattan. While the rest of us waited for our plates of Danish breakfast, Francky Knapp had shuffled off to the bathroom, then returned to the table with newfound excitement at this unexpected find. Naturally, I, too, had to see it for myself. The slab of stone occupied the entire industrial-style basin, a patch of rust-colored mineral deposits at its center where the water hit. Weird! I thought, then I put it out of my mind for months. That was until I met a friend for coffee at the location of Rhythm Zero in Greenpoint, Brooklyn, which looks more like a room in an art museum than a coffee shop. There, a large hunk of stone sat in front of a large mirror next to the counter. Yet another imposed itself in the bathroom, positioned between the sink and the toilet, as though natural absorption for dripping hands making the trip to the hand dryer. Two establishments with big decorative rocks: a coincidence, or an affectation? But then, I found myself in Pizza 4P’s, an ambitiously and intricately designed pizza import from Vietnam for which six literal boulders were transported into the restaurant from a stone wholesaler in New Jersey. Now three spots? There’s something going on there. It’s at Pizza 4P’s, which opened this summer in Brooklyn in a high-ceilinged industrial space, where this trend can be found at its extreme. When you open the door, you’re greeted by a host stand in the form of a large, tablelike boulder. The stone, which was forklifted in, was chosen for this usage because of its waist height and the natural notch in its corner, perfect for holding menus. An adjacent stone, lower and smaller, acts as a bench for diners waiting for their table. Four more boulders erupt from the space, forcing the layout of the large dining room into a snaking path. “After we found the stones, we changed the position,” global branding director Kazuya Kubota explained to me over a tour of the space. None have been cut into shape; they have all been chosen for their size and form, and then the restaurant designed around them. Some of the stones sprout thick metal support wires, allowing them to weigh down the wooden frames along the walls that hold hanging plants. The largest stone — at around two tons, toward the center of the dining room, with a table butting up against it — is comparable in weight to the pizza oven, according to Kubota. Along with all the hanging plants, the stones give the otherwise industrial space a semblance of nature, bridging the gap between Brooklyn urbanism and the pastoral settings of the farms listed on the menu. For her rocks, Ivana Somorai, who owns Rhythm Zero, was inspired by the use of natural materials in Japanese design. She told me over email that she also wanted to bring a “natural, unexpected element” into the shop’s interiors. Initially, the Greenpoint location featured several rocks, minimal seating, and a large tangerine tree. When she redesigned the interior — it now features a large couch and more seating — the rocks stayed, mostly because they were too heavy. “I knew they would not be leaving the space for a while,” Somorai wrote. Since then, rocks have become a memorable feature of the cafe. (Every location looks different; all are very stylish, some feature stones.) The one next to the mirror “unexpectedly became a favorite sitting area for our regulars,” Somorai explains. “The rocks began as part of a specific design moment, but they ended up becoming part of the life of the cafe and the way people use the space.” As for why the second rock ended up in the bathroom… well, isn’t that kind of the last thing you’d expect? “I wanted people to be surprised when they opened the door: The bathroom is dark, and then there is this large rock. I wanted them to be like, ‘Why is there a rock here?’” Somorai wrote. (Yes, I had that thought.) I imagine this desire to pique curiosity is part of the rationale at Gem, too. While I couldn’t get ahold of McGarry to know more about the Gem stone [ba-dum-tss], his representative told me via email that, to his recollection, “Gem Home, [the now-closed] Gem Wine, and I think Cove all had/have rocks in their restroom sinks.” This really only opens up more questions though; if only I could have asked them! As for Pizza 4P’s, those big rocks fit into a bigger philosophy. The chain has dozens of locations in different countries. Each location is unique — its art, furniture, and space designed entirely custom (boulders in Brooklyn doesn’t mean stones in Cambodia). Each country is guided by a different theme. In Indonesia, that’s biodiversity; in the United States, it’s the idea of “what the earth told me.” To that end, they thought of the stones like they did ingredients, Kubota explains: The goal is to find something beautiful in nature and then work around it. Alas, on my most recent visit to Rhythm Zero in Greenpoint, the rock outside the bathroom was gone. Apparently, that was part of an even more recent renovation. The rocks were moved to the nearby Transmitter Park. Somorai described it as “where they belong, I guess.”

item.title: Hoy Is Bringing Night-Market Energy to NYC
item.description:
Source: Eater Score: 2.20
This excerpt was originally published in Pre Shift, our newsletter for the hospitality industry. Subscribe for more first-person accounts, advice, and interviews. This is the first installment of our series Getting on the Map, presented by Apple Maps. Over the next three weeks, we’ll be sharing how some of the most creative bars and restaurants are marketing themselves to stand out in a crowded hospitality scene. When I spoke with Cyed Adraincem, he apologized for stumbling over any words; he’d been up at 4 a.m. to wash the sidewalk in front of his forthcoming restaurant. “I wanted to beat all the foot traffic,” he said. Adraincem seems to have brought that same dedication to outfitting Hoy, which will serve Filipino street food in a Manila night-market-like space. Though not yet open, the restaurant has already garnered a lot of attention for its loud and off-kilter aesthetic, smart pop cultural ties, and behind-the-scenes peeks into R&D. I asked him about designing the space, the merch plan, and how opening is going. Mary Anne Porto: Can you tell us about the restaurant concept? Cyed Adraincem: It’s Filipino street food, super fast casual. I’m trying to introduce Filipino food to a broader audience because I feel like we’re underrepresented in New York City. We’ll be serving barbecue skewers, lumpia, and a couple different sandwiches. It’s a pretty simple menu, nothing too fancy, mostly traditional, with chef techniques that we’ve learned over the years. I think the New York dining scene wants something more casual, more affordable right now. They don’t want something pretentious; they just want to eat and have a good drink. The space is based on American diners because I love them. I’ve also been working in cocktail bars for the past seven years. So if you come into the restaurant, it’s kind of a mashup of the two. Those two things [feel similar] to the Manila night market [theme] we’re going for. It’s very high energy; everyone is front-facing; it’s loud and fun. Since everything is counter service, everything is front-facing. The kitchen is open, so I think the energy will keep going throughout the restaurant. We’ll communicate in front of everyone, and it’ll be like a street-market affair. How did you come up with the branding and logo for Hoy? My designer is Kristofferson San Pablo. He’s a Filipino American, and he’s actually my cousin. He’s a well-known artist in LA. We decided on this design based on all the intense fun of a Manila night market. So there are a lot of different colors, a lot of visually stimulating stuff, without being too overwhelming. The pattern on the walls comes from one of the oldest textile patterns in the Philippines. It was an easy choice to showcase our culture in a cool way. [We have] shelves of snacks that are supposed to mimic a sari-sari store in the Philippines. They are usually on every street corner and typically operating right out of the owner’s home, selling an assortment of everyday essentials. Cookbooks [on the shelves were] passed down from my parents. Some of them are very old. They are the baseline of what we will be creating for the restaurant. We also have cookbooks from our local favorites. We tried to stay away from the typical Filipino [branding] stuff, like the star and the sun and barong tagalogs, things that are very obviously Filipino. We wanted to use things like the barrel man, carabao [water buffalo], farmer life, which are a little bit different from the mainstream. I love the barrel man. It’s super Filipino culture. And the other fun part of it is I get to teach people who don’t know about this. These barrel men were made-to-sell souvenirs for poor people to make money. But it’s also how Filipinos act: It’s fun, it’s a gag gift. I also have a bunch of art pieces from different artists around the city and LA as well. We’re going to try to stick with as much Filipino art as we can, but I’m open to [any artists]. As long as it’s local and made with community in mind, I’m happy to support them. Before even opening, you’ve channeled these pop-culture moments through some of your designs, like your Knicks-themed choking sign. How quickly can you and your designer put together this art, and what’s the process like? Everything’s on the fly, baby. Kris’ art is very pop-culture heavy. For him, it’s kind of second nature. I bring things up, and he’s like “Oh yeah, I’ve already been working on something like that.” He keeps up with all of it. He works fast. What merch are you planning to have? A bunch of different things. We entertained the idea of making our own barrel man, or barrel man key chains, and even house slippers. Our standard products we’ll probably carry are shirts, hats, and totes, and we’ll probably cater to the season. As we get open and understand the space better, we’ll start producing more merch. It’s going to be fun, and most of this merch is going to be collaborative with other artists and creatives, too. Some restaurants open with a bare-bones design while they get their footing, then expand into merch as they grow. But it seems like you’re going all-in with your opening, with a very designed space and a merch line. Why did you decide to do that? I’ve been in the industry for almost 17 years. And working in cocktail bars for seven of those, I saw that merch was flying off the shelves. Bartenders were always wearing other bars’ shirts, representing other industry spots. I think more people are wearing clothes that [signify] places that they love. I see Kikkoman jackets and T-shirts from all of my favorite restaurants, and that’s all I wear, too. So I thought it was important to spread the word, and eventually have it as another outlet of revenue. How did you approach the inside of the restaurant? Realistically, [furnishing a restaurant] is a lot of legwork. Everything is so expensive right now. It’s probably the worst time to open a restaurant. So it’s about doing your due diligence and comparing prices. I go to Home Depot, Amazon, The Container Store and see who has the best price, then go from there, so it’s a lot of searching and researching. And everything on the shelves is pretty personal: knickknacks and art from friends and family. We’ll also have a lot of vegetation to try to mimic the tropical Philippines. We made a pot pond out of a large planter pot, and we’re currently growing lemongrass, a calamansi tree, and labuyo chiles in a garden next to the pond. We’re in a corner building, so we get lots of light. We’re going to make a jungle and grow and eat what we can. What’s your path to opening look like right now? We have an issue with our gas firing with the DOB [New York’s Department of Buildings] right now, so we can’t cook onsite until it gets all sorted out. Until then, we decided to open up for the community and have a residency in the space. We’re [hosting] Arellano Pandesal from Queens, which does Filipino pastries, while we do the beverages. We’re also planning to launch a community market place with local vendors and friends and family. It’s a good way to get people in the space and get people excited.

item.title: Grog almighty – the rise and rise of navy-strength gin
item.description:
Source: Food & Drink Score: 3.56
Grog almighty – the rise and rise of navy-strength gin Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. Old Raj gin looks like the kind of thing you’d find at the back of your grandfather’s drinks cabinet; its mercantile font and black-and-white portrait of a colonial officer are from another age. Launched in 1972 by Scotland’s oldest independent whisky bottlers, Cadenhead’s, the saffron-laced gin spent decades being resolutely uncool. So I was astonished to find, on a recent trip to New York, that it’s now a cult Martini pour. William Elliott, bar director of Brooklyn’s Maison Premiere, was an early adopter of Old Raj. “We were hunting down obscure, overproof [high abv] gins for a tableside Martini and were struck by its quiet intensity,” he says. “The luxurious application of saffron gives it a tonal and textural quality that was a clear upgrade from the brutishness of most London Dry-style gins.” Old Raj is bottled at two strengths: 46 per cent (Red Label, £30) and a bracing 55 per cent (Blue Label, £34). “The 55 per cent abv version is the must-have,” says Nima Ansari, spirits buyer at Manhattan’s Astor Wines. The fact Old Raj is owned by the company that distils the Campbeltown single malt Springbank is also, he says, a plus for spirits connoisseurs. Blue Label is what they use for Martinis at Maison Premiere and Le Veau d’Or on Manhattan’s Upper East Side. You’ll also see it on the list at Gallaghers Steakhouse, Death & Co and Frenchette, where it’s served in a Martini twist with vermouth and tomato water. “I first came across Old Raj while working at Small Victory in Austin, Texas,” says Jojo Colonna, bar director at Four Horsemen’s buzzing Italian I Cavallini in Brooklyn. If a customer requested Blue Label, he says, “it was a sign of an intentional Martini drinker”. Old-style, high-strength gins have been making a comeback among Martini connoisseurs. “At the higher abv, the spirit holds on to more of those botanical oils and aromas,” says James Stevenson, founder of new Martini bar Brutes of Mayfair, where the house gin is Plymouth Navy Strength (£42), a 57 per cent abv homage to the high-proof gins once drunk by officers in the Royal Navy. “You still get a very dry, clean Martini, but with a much more oily texture, from the gin.” If you’re mixing Martinis with a high-strength gin, “stir with ice for longer than usual to allow for adequate dilution”, advises Kevin Beary, beverage director of Chicago’s Kitty’s Cosmopolitan Club. Erik Delanoy of Elder in NYC also recommends using Old Raj Blue Label for a wet Martini with equal parts gin and vermouth. At Three Sheets in Soho, they favour The Botanist’s 50 per cent abv Distiller’s Strength (£42). “It’s still very soft and mellow,” says co-owner Max Venning. “Because it’s higher-proof, you can stir it down for longer and get the Martini really cold, without losing the lovely wild, floral botanicals.” Forget old-school stiffener – it’s now all about soft power. item.title: Louis Thompson – fashion’s favourite pastry chef
item.description:
Source: Food & Drink Score: 3.21
Louis Thompson – fashion’s favourite pastry chef Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. Louis Thompson is sitting in a brightly lit hallway in central London, “wearing my chef whites, which have come straight out of the kitchen”, he says excitedly. He is rakishly handsome and 6ft 2in tall, and his faint Australian accent and youth are evident. His whereabouts – the brightly lit kitchen of Spring, the critically lauded restaurant where he’s freelancing today – are more nondescript. “I’m just piping some chocolate sprinkles, because Spring would never buy chocolate sprinkles,” he jokes. “We make them by hand with beautiful Mexican chilli and vanilla.” Since arriving from his native Melbourne in 2019, 28-year-old Thompson has become one of London’s most in-demand pastry chefs. The month we speak, he’s spent countless hours churning 100 kilos of ice cream for a private summer party at the Serpentine Pavilion, baked three single-layer cakes for the wedding of Quince Bakery founder Anna Higham, and shared a recipe for elderflower fritters with fellow pastry chef Nicola Lamb’s more than 100,000 Substack subscribers. This month he’ll join Helen Goh at Quince Bakery in Islington to discuss her new book, Baking & the Meaning of Life (Murdoch). Pastry cheffing aside, Thompson is a rising model who has worked for Simone Rocha and Stefan Cooke. (He inaugurated the latter’s AW25 collection with a nearly metre-wide cherry and almond cake.) Now, having signed with Next London modelling agency, he hopes to learn from the various creatives in his network. “He just hits the nail on the head every time,” says Stefan Cooke co-founder Jake Burt, who has been serving Thompson’s pastries with black coffee and Marlboro Reds at his cult east London shop Jake’s since 2024. He saw Thompson at a Stefan Cooke event in 2023, which led to the model’s first print campaign, and recruited him to do the cakes. Thompson credits his late father – “a fiercely intelligent man” who received an Order of Australia for his work with marginalised communities – for his love of cooking. At home, food was a “pathway to curiosity and access”, he says. A rhubarb tart became a lesson about rationing in the second world war. Strawberries tossed with heaps of brown sugar and balsamic vinegar taught him to conjure magic from unfussy ingredients. Thompson’s mother, a lecturer in architecture at RMIT University, instilled in him “neatness, care and diligence”, something evidenced in his signature galettes, a traditionally entry-level pastry, which in his hands becomes a Michelin-level dish. Only a few years ago, Thompson was working at a call centre in Melbourne, trying to save money in order to move London to study fashion history and theory at Central Saint Martins. He’d devour cookbooks and stay up until the early hours baking and icing cakes with a colleague to unwind. “What drew me to baking was that it was more process-driven [than cooking],” he says. “In baking, you use raw ingredients combined in a specific way to transform them. The timelines are generally longer and you’re often bringing different elements together.” Thompson baked part-time while juggling his studies. A three-month stint making bagels at a café led to a job at Violet London, the California-style bakery where he learned the art of icing cakes. Three years later, in 2023, he was referred to Spring. The restaurant’s late chef-patron Skye Gyngell – “the most charismatic person I ever met” – praised him for his curiosity. “Food-wise, she definitely taught me subtlety,” Thompson reflects. “As a younger chef, I thought being skilled meant being able to turn the flavour dials up to 100. Skye taught me how to arrange flavour with more harmony.” Back then, it looked as if Thompson would have to choose between food and fashion; today his remit allows him to do both. “It’s simply another form of communication,” he says of his modelling. His ability to straddle both industries is reflective of a time where the worlds of fashion and culinary arts have become closely interlinked. “Combining food and fashion is a way of creating intimacy around something that can otherwise feel quite untouchable,” says cake artist Sophia Stolz, who bakes for brands including Miu Miu, Dior and Gucci. “Food is incredibly universal; luxury fashion is not. Food creates a common ground between a brand and the person experiencing it.” Thompson is content for his two pursuits to keep evolving. “I’ve spent a long time connecting all sorts of random dots,” he says. “Now I’m at a point where those dots and connections form a cohesive web.” Most recently he’s started contributing to AnOther Magazine’s new food column. A commission for American comedian Cole Escola is also on deck. In December, he’ll travel home and host events with local chefs he admires. “I try to sniff out new information wherever it might be,” he says. “I always seek out new experiences – and go into them with openness.” Comments

item.title: Affordable Alternatives to Japan's Most Crowded Destinations
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 7.71
Japan welcomed more visitors in 2025 than ever before, and most walked the same ten streets. The crowding is real but concentrated: a few temples, villages, and viewpoints absorb most of it, while places offering the same experience sit half empty a valley away. Budget travelers hear a tempting promise: quieter must mean cheaper. Sometimes it does. Sometimes the quiet option adds a shinkansen leg or a rural bus that erases every yen saved on admission. The only way to know is to do the math, so this article does it for four popular swaps using prices checked in August 2026 from official sources. That timing matters: JR East raised fares on March 14, 2026, and Kyoto doubled its accommodation tax two weeks earlier, so numbers from older guides are quietly wrong. The pairings come from the Crowd-Free Japan Index, which matches 40 of Japan's most-visited places with curated quieter alternatives. Kanazawa Instead of Kyoto: The Savings Are on the Ground, Not the Rails Kanazawa is often called "little Kyoto," which annoys both cities, but the comparison holds where it counts. The Higashi Chaya geisha district is a smaller, calmer Gion where the teahouses actually let you in: Ochaya Shima charges ¥500 to walk through a working 1820s interior. In contrast, most Gion teahouses remain entirely closed to casual visitors. Omicho Market delivers the seafood-breakfast experience of Tokyo's Tsukiji Outer Market, with locals still doing their shopping there, and entry to Kenroku-en, one of Japan's three great gardens, costs ¥320, compared with ¥500 for Kinkaku-ji or ¥500 for Kiyomizu-dera, each ticketed separately. The biggest savings come from where you sleep. Kyoto's average hotel rate hit a record ¥20,195 per night in 2024. Since March 1, 2026, the city has charged a ¥1,000 per-person-per-night accommodation tax on rooms priced at ¥20,000-49,999, double the previous rate. Kanazawa's tax on the same room is ¥500. | Cost item (August 2026) | Kyoto | Kanazawa | | Shinkansen from Tokyo, one way | ¥14,170 | ¥14,600 | | City bus, single ride | ¥230 | ¥220 | | Transit day pass | ¥1,100 | ¥800 | | Headline garden or temple | ¥500 | ¥320 | | Accommodation tax, per person | ¥1,000 p.p. per night | ¥500 p.p. per night | Note the first row: The train from Tokyo to Kanazawa costs slightly more than the train to Kyoto. The swap pays off in everything after you arrive and compounds with every night you stay. Shima Onsen Instead of Ginzan Onsen: The Clearest Budget Win in Japan Ginzan Onsen's gaslit street has become so popular that the town now meters its own visitors. In winter, day visitors park two kilometers out and ride a shuttle; evening entry requires a paid reservation (¥1,150 in the first season, capped at 100 people per hour), and after 8 pm the street closes to everyone but overnight guests. Those overnight stays start at roughly ¥25,000 per person with meals, and reaching the town from Tokyo costs about ¥13,000 by the Yamagata Shinkansen, plus a ¥1,000 bus that takes cash only. Shima Onsen, tucked in a Gunma river gorge, offers the same Taisho-era wooden-ryokan romance with none of the metering. Sekizenkan's main building dates to 1691, making it Japan's oldest hot-spring inn building, and it is often said to have inspired the bathhouse in Spirited Away; its budget rooms start at ¥10,450 per person. The riverside cave bath Kawara-no-yu is open to day visitors from 9:00 to 15:00 without charge. Best of all, a direct highway bus runs from Tokyo Station for ¥3,500 one way and ¥6,300 round trip, about three and a half hours. | Cost item (August 2026) | Ginzan Onsen | Shima Onsen | | Transport from Tokyo, one way | ~¥14,000 (shinkansen + bus) | ¥3,500 (direct bus) | | Night in a heritage ryokan | From ~¥25,000 p.p. with meals | From ¥10,450 p.p. at Sekizenkan | | Soaking without staying | Winter evenings ticketed | Free cave bath, 9:00–15:00 | One honest caveat: the bus runs once daily each way and must be reserved by 4 pm the day before. If you miss it, the rail route via Nakanojo costs more and takes longer. Book the seat, then relax. Ainokura Instead of Shirakawa-go: Let Your Routing Decide Shirakawa-go itself is not the budget problem; walking the village is free, the Wada House costs ¥400, and the viewpoint shuttle costs ¥300. The problem is that everyone arrives on the same reservation-only buses (¥2,800 one way from either Kanazawa or Takayama) and shares the lanes with them. Ainokura, a village of twenty thatched gassho-zukuri farmhouses on a mountainside in neighboring Gokayama, is listed as a World Heritage site with a fraction of the foot traffic. It is also free to enter on foot, and the World Heritage Bus from Takaoka or Shin-Takaoka costs ¥1,100, less than half the Shirakawa-go fare. Whether that saves you money depends entirely on your routing. Traveling the Hokuriku Shinkansen anyway? Step off at Shin-Takaoka and Ainokura is the cheaper, quieter choice. Based in Kanazawa or Takayama with no plans northward? The extra rail leg to Takaoka eats the difference, so the direct ¥2,800 bus to Shirakawa-go wins. The best-value option for seeing both: the ¥4,000 two-day unlimited pass covers Ainokura, Suganuma, and Shirakawa-go on one ticket, and costs less than buying a single round trip separately. Related: Travelers looking beyond Tokyo and Kyoto can find more ideas in Go Backpacking's guide to Japan's Chubu region. Naoshima and Teshima Instead of teamLab: When Quieter Costs More Honesty requires one counterexample, because quiet does not automatically mean cheap. Tokyo's teamLab Planets charges from ¥3,600, with date-based pricing. The contemplative alternatives are Naoshima and Teshima, neighboring art islands in the Seto Inland Sea: the Chichu Art Museum costs ¥2,500-3,000 with timed reservations that cap visitors. The Teshima Art Museum costs ¥1,800-2,000. The direct ferry from Uno Port to Naoshima costs ¥370, while the ferry to Teshima costs ¥780. Per ticket, the islands undercut teamLab. Per trip, they usually don't: Uno Port is a Shinkansen ride and two local connections from Tokyo, and that transport dwarfs the admission savings. The swap only makes financial sense when Setouchi is already on your route, say between Osaka and Hiroshima. If it is, take it without hesitation; if not, this is the case where the crowded option is genuinely the affordable one. The Cheapest Alternative: Don't Leave the City You're In The most expensive way to escape a crowd is to cross half of Honshu. A same-day dash from Tokyo to Kyoto for Fushimi Inari's torii gates costs over ¥28,000 in return shinkansen fares before you have eaten anything. Meanwhile, Nezu Shrine, one of Tokyo's oldest, has its own tunnel of vermilion torii at the Otome Inari sub-shrine, costs nothing to enter, and sits a ¥180 metro ride from central Tokyo. The same logic covers bamboo. Kamakura's Hokoku-ji temple has a grove where you can sit with matcha for ¥400 admission plus ¥600 for the tea. The Great Buddha at Kotoku-in across town charges ¥300, and the train from Tokyo costs ¥1,040. That makes a full bamboo-and-Buddha day out possible for under ¥5,000, compared with visiting Arashiyama's grove at the far end of a ¥28,000 round trip. Even garden-hopping scales down: Kiyosumi Garden charges ¥150 for stone-hopping across carp ponds that Shinjuku Gyoen crowds pay ¥500 for. Altitude works the same way. Shibuya Sky's rooftop charges ¥2,700 online for daytime entry and ¥3,400 for sunset slots, and shares the deck with everyone else who booked the same golden hour. Sunshine 60's Tenbou-Park observatory in Ikebukuro shows a comparable skyline for ¥700 on weekdays, and the free 26th-floor observation lobby of Carrot Tower in Sangenjaya, a few minutes from Shibuya on the Den-en-toshi line, faces Mount Fuji at sunset and charges nothing at all. Four Rules Before You Swap - Price the final leg first. Rural alternatives live or die by the last bus or ferry: its fare and, above all, its schedule. One missed daily departure can force a taxi that costs more than the whole day. - Admission is rarely the problem. Japanese entry fees are modest: ¥150-800 covers most of the attractions in this article. Accommodation and intercity trains decide your budget, so compare hotel rates and lodging taxes before temple tickets. For a broader breakdown of travel costs, read Go Backpacking's guide to backpacking Japan on a budget. - Some crowded icons are free. Fushimi Inari charges nothing; Shirakawa-go's lanes charge nothing. Swapping away from them buys you a better experience, not a cheaper one. Know which reward you're paying for. - Recheck prices from 2026 onward. The March 2026 JR East fare rise and Kyoto's doubled accommodation tax made many older budget guides inaccurate. The official links above reflect August 2026 prices. Quiet and cheap usually travel together in Japan, but not always, and never automatically. Run the numbers for your own route, and you'll often find the lesser-known option costs less and gives more. When it doesn't, at least you'll know before the bus timetable tells you.

item.title: Kilimanjaro Routes Compared: Which Should You Choose?
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 6.47
Seven official routes lead up Kilimanjaro, and most people narrow their choice to two or three within an hour of reading about them. Machame is the popular one, Lemosho the scenic one, Marangu the one where you sleep in huts instead of tents. Those labels are accurate but don't affect whether you reach the summit. Kilimanjaro is 5,895 m (19,341 ft) high. Its standard trekking routes do not require technical climbing equipment (ropes, an ice axe), but the extreme altitude makes acclimatization essential. The number of days on the mountain matters. Five-day itineraries leave less time for acclimatization, while some operators report summit success rates around 95% on eight-day climbs. These are operator-reported figures, not mountain-wide averages. The takeaway is simple: allow your body more time to adapt before summit night. How the Routes Actually Work Seven official ascent routes exist, but they don't stay separate all the way up. Every climb has three phases, and the route you choose changes each of them differently. The approach (the first four to six days) is where the routes differ. Lemosho starts in quiet rainforest on the western flank. Rongai comes from the dry northern side near the Kenyan border. Machame and Marangu climb from the busy south. For four to six days, you circle toward Kibo, the main volcanic cone, gaining altitude through rainforest, moorland, and alpine desert. This is where you acclimatize, so the number of days here matters most. Summit night. The approaches converge toward Kibo, with most standard itineraries using one of two main summit routes. If you came via Machame, Lemosho, Shira, or Umbwe, you leave Barafu Camp around midnight, climb to Stella Point, then walk the crater rim to Uhuru Peak. Marangu and Rongai climbers leave Kibo Hut, and their route to Gilman's Point takes longer because much of it runs over loose volcanic scree. Either way, you gain about 1,200 meters in the dark. The Western Breach is another summit route, but rockfall and unstable ice make it risky. For that reason, careful operators avoid it. The descent. The park separates uphill and downhill traffic. Routes that summit from Barafu come down the Mweka corridor, a trail used only for going down. Marangu and Rongai climbers walk back down the Marangu trail, sharing it with groups heading up. The Routes, Side by Side | Route | Days | Start from | Sleeping | Traffic | Pick it if | | Machame ("Whiskey") | 7 (or 6) | South | Tents | High | You want the classic climb-high-sleep-low profile and the Barranco Wall, and crowds don't bother you. | | Lemosho | 8 (or 7) | West | Tents | Low early, medium later | It's your first high-altitude climb, and you can spare the extra day. | | Marangu ("Coca-Cola") | 6 (or 5) | Southeast | Wooden huts | High | Sleeping in a tent is not an option for you. | | Rongai | 6 | North | Tents | Low | You want quiet, or you're climbing during the short rains. | | Northern Circuit | 8–9 | West, then north | Tents | Very low | You prioritize extra acclimatization time and a quieter approach. | | Umbwe | 6 | South | Tents | Very low | You're already acclimatized and want a steep, direct route. | | Londorossi (Shira) | 6–8 | West, by vehicle to the plateau | Tents | Very low | You want open views from day one and understand the altitude trade-off. | Route by Route Machame: the "Whiskey Route" (7 days) Machame is the most popular route on the mountain, and the nickname compares it to Marangu, the "Coca-Cola Route." The key differences are that Machame is tougher and steeper, and you sleep in tents. In seven days, you pass through every climate zone Kilimanjaro has, from wet rainforest at 1,800 meters to the frozen crater rim. The third day takes you up to Lava Tower at 4,600 meters and then down to Barranco Camp at 3,900 meters to sleep. That is the "climb high, sleep low" principle built into the route, which is why Machame acclimatizes people so well despite its pace. The next morning you scramble the Barranco Wall, a near-vertical face that needs hands for balance but no rope. The downside is traffic. Machame and Marangu take the lion's share of expeditions, and you will share camps with hundreds of other climbers. The Barranco Wall gives the climb real mountaineering character, and the scenery earns the route its reputation. Still, anyone choosing Machame has to be willing to move in a stream of other groups and share the intermediate camps. The other decision on Machame is between six and seven days. The difference is a single night at Karanga Camp after the Barranco Wall. Drop it, and you go straight from the wall to Barafu and into summit night on the same push, when accumulated fatigue shows up. For example, ALPO runs the Machame Route on the seven-day schedule and keeps that Karanga night for this reason; the company reports 95-97% of its climbers reaching the summit on that version. Its guidance on the six-day option is that the success rate is lower. Lemosho (8 days) Lemosho starts on the remote western flank at Londorossi Gate, about three hours' drive from Moshi. The first two days run through rainforest that the southern routes never touch, and you may not see another group. This is where you are most likely to see colobus monkeys. The route then crosses the Shira Plateau from west to east, one of the highest plateaus on Earth, and on the eight-day version you spend two nights up there, at Shira 1 (3,500 m) and Shira 2 (3,840 m). That slow gain is the whole point. From the plateau, Lemosho joins the Machame trail, so the Lava Tower day, the Barranco Wall, and the summit night are the same. The main decision on Lemosho is whether to do seven or eight days. Dropping to seven means crossing Shira in one long stage and losing a night of adaptation, which helps most. Lemosho also costs more than Machame, partly because of the long drive to a remote trailhead and partly because the extra day adds food and crew wages. For someone whose first real altitude climb is this one, the eight-day Lemosho remains the most balanced option; the gain comes slowly enough that your body has time to catch up. Marangu: the "Coca-Cola Route" (6 days) Marangu is the only route where you sleep in permanent wooden huts instead of tents. The huts are dorm-style, with anywhere from 4 to 20 people per room and shared bathrooms. It is also the historic original route and the one with the gentlest approach gradient, which is how it got its reputation as the easy one. That reputation can be misleading: a gentler trail does not remove altitude challenges. If you prefer hut accommodation, compare daily sleeping altitudes and acclimatization opportunities carefully, and favor the six-day itinerary over the five-day version. Summit night climbs from Kibo Hut toward Gilman's Point, and the route uses the same trail for ascent and descent, so you meet descending groups on your way up. The sensible rule is to choose Marangu in exactly one case, when a tent is physically or psychologically not an option for you, and then to take six days, never five. Rongai (6 days) Rongai approaches from the north, close to the Kenyan border, after a long drive to the trailhead. The northern flank is drier, making Rongai the sensible pick if climbing during the short rains in November. It is also the quietest standard route, with a real chance of larger wildlife on the lower section. The early terrain is less dramatic than on the western routes, and summit night from Kibo Hut is long and monotonous. It is probably the most undervalued route on the mountain: introverted, wild, and worth the trade for silence. Editor's note: For a firsthand perspective, read this account of climbing Kilimanjaro via the Rongai Route, from life at camp to the midnight summit push. Northern Circuit (8-9 days) The Northern Circuit is one of the longest itinerary options, giving you more time to acclimatize. As a result, it has one of the higher summit rates. It starts on the western side, like Lemosho, then swings around the northern face of Kibo on a nearly empty traverse before rejoining the main trails for the summit push. The extra days provide more time to adapt, although individual responses to altitude vary. It is generally among the more expensive options because you are paying for a longer expedition, and it requires solid multi-day trekking endurance. If reliably reaching Uhuru Peak is the goal and time is not the constraint, this is the route. Umbwe and Londorossi (Shira) Umbwe is the steepest line on the mountain and the most direct, climbing a narrow forest ridge that almost no one else uses. Its rapid ascent leaves little time to acclimatize, making it a better option for trekkers who are already acclimatized. Previous altitude experience alone is not a substitute. Londorossi, sometimes called the Shira Route, approaches from the west but begins with a vehicle transfer straight onto the Shira Plateau at 3,400 meters. The views open from day one. You give up the gradual gain that every other route builds in, which is worth considering before you book. What To Weigh Before You Book Days on the mountain. When comparing itineraries, prioritize acclimatization time. Look beyond total trip length to daily sleeping altitudes and acclimatization opportunities. Extra time helps, but fitness and previous altitude experience do not guarantee protection from altitude illness. Follow your guide's safety advice and be prepared to turn around. That is not a guidebook opinion. Yevgen Staroselskiy, co-founder of ALPO Guided Expeditions, is a Master of Sport in Mountaineering and holder of the "Snow Leopard" title (#376), with more than 130 major climbs behind him, including Everest (8,848 m, 29,029 ft) and K2 (8,611 m, 28,251 ft), and 25+ groups guided to the top of Kilimanjaro. His view of the time question is blunt: I've climbed Everest and K2, and I can tell you that no route on Kilimanjaro needs that kind of preparation. What it does need is that you take the altitude seriously. Give your body the days, walk slowly, and almost any physically active person will reach Uhuru Peak. Where I see people fail is when they try to save a day. - Yevgen Staroselskiy, Master of Sport in Mountaineering, co-founder of ALPO Guided Expeditions Everything else on this list is secondary to that number. Tent or hut. A binary question, and it settles Marangu yes-or-no before anything else. Crowds. Machame and Marangu are busy. Rongai and the Northern Circuit are not. Lemosho is quiet for two days and then joins the Machame stream. Summit night profile. From Barafu, the climb to Stella Point is steeper, but you are mostly on firm ground. From Kibo Hut, you spend more hours on scree before you reach Gilman's Point. Season. Compare expected rainfall and trail conditions for your travel dates with your operator. Wetter periods mean muddy trails and reduced visibility; the northern approach is generally drier. Conditions vary, so avoid treating any seasonal window as a guarantee of dry weather. The dry windows are June to early October and mid-December to early April. During the short rains in November, the northern side stays drier, which is a point in Rongai's favor. In April and May, the trails wash out, and clouds hide the views, so no route is worth doing then. A Quick Decision Guide - First high-altitude climb and you can spare eight days: Lemosho. - Seven days, and sharing camp with other groups does not bother you: Machame, on the seven-day schedule rather than six. - You will not sleep in a tent: Marangu, six days, no shorter. - Climbing in November, or you want the mountain mostly to yourself: Rongai. - More time for acclimatization and a quieter approach: Northern Circuit. Whichever route you choose, prioritize an itinerary that allows time to acclimatize rather than booking the shortest option. This article was published in partnership with ALPO Guided Expeditions.

item.title: Theo James Shares His Restaurant’s Burro e Parmigiano Recipe
item.description:
Source: NYT > Dining & Wine Score: 2.45
Advertisement Theo James loves to cook based on vibes.“I don’t do it with exactitude because I’m too impatient,” Mr. James said. He extends that approach to burro e parmigiano, a simple Northern Italian dish that happens to be one of his favorites. (It’s also a recipe he makes for his kids, he told Cathy Lo, a New York Times Cooking editor.) Recipe: Theo James’s Burro e Parmigiano While he may not be one for measurements, when he makes his version, which is adapted from Ornella, a restaurant he owns with Naz Hassan and Ed Templeton in East London, he does make sure the ingredients are the best they can be: deeply flavored dark chicken stock, aged Parmesan, fresh tagliatelle. When simplicity and incredible ingredients meet, he said, “those things bound together create something incredibly delicious.” You can watch him cook the dish alongside Kaya Scodelario, his co-star in Guy Ritchie’s comedy-drama series “The Gentlemen” and another passionate cook, in the video below (or on YouTube). Here are excerpts from the interview and the outtakes, which have been edited and condensed. Have you ever cooked with each other before today? THEO JAMES No, but you keep threatening to cook me Brazilian. KAYA SCODELARIO I want to cook dinner for you, but you don’t ever answer my calls. JAMES Kaya’s a great Brazilian chef. What’s your favorite thing to cook? SCODELARIO I just like home comfort food. When I’m working, I really miss cooking — when I’m away in hotels and stuff and traveling. So when I get home, it’s the first thing I want to do: spend four hours in the kitchen just cooking. Podcast, glass of wine, no one disturbing me and, yeah, cooking for people. It’s my love language. I like to feed. Have either of you ever worked in the food service industry? JAMES Yes. SCODELARIO Did you? JAMES Yeah. God, yeah. I was a waiter in multiple pubs. I even did one of those things where you had to turn up to catering venues — SCODELARIO Silver service? JAMES No. God, no. You turn up as kind of a teenager. I’ll always remember — I had all of the pinnies on — and I leant over to pour someone some coffee, and I had another coffee pot in my left hand, and I poured the coffee all over the guy’s crotch, basically. I got instantly fired. Cheers! SCODELARIO I’ve never worked in the service industry. JAMES Have you not? SCODELARIO No, I never. But I played a waitress, and I was really bad at it. I couldn’t carry the [tray]. What’s the best or worst food you’ve ever had to do a scene with? SCODELARIO We, on “Maze Runner,” had to do a scene where we hadn’t had food for ages, and we walk in a room, and there’s every kind of food imaginable. They let us choose, and I wanted deep-fried Oreos. But I got really sick because I had about seven of them straight away. So that was great but also awful. How do you feel about eating food in bed? SCODELARIO I’m down for eating food in bed. JAMES Really? I’ve always felt kind of repulsed by the idea of it. SCODELARIO OK. [Both laugh] SCODELARIO I think it’s always a better idea than the reality of it. Like, you know, on Mother’s Day or Father’s Day, where they’re like, “Oh, we’ll do Mummy’s breakfast in bed.” And you’re like, This is actually annoying because now I’m stuck in the bed, and there’s orange juice everywhere. JAMES That’s cute. Yeah, but I don’t like the idea of scoffing sandwiches while you’re asleep. SCODELARIO What about in a hotel? JAMES Hotel, you’re allowed to do for breakfast, but that’s it. SCODELARIO OK. What about a midday club sandwich? You wouldn’t eat that on the bed? JAMES Maybe near the bed, or adjacent to the bed, but never in the bed. If the cast of “The Gentlemen” owned a restaurant, what would everyone’s roles be? SCODELARIO I’d like you as the angry chef in the background. You don’t ever want to come out and see people, but you’re really stressed all the time. JAMES What would Joely [Richardson] — what would her role be? SCODELARIO Front of house. JAMES What would your role be? Manager. SCODELARIO No. JAMES It’s a bit boring. SCODELARIO I’d be … I don’t know. Keep the books. In your family, do you have any specific traditions around food? JAMES You have good traditions from your mother in your family about food, right? SCODELARIO Kind of. We do Christmas on Christmas Eve instead of Christmas Day. We eat, like, I think, three or four times a week Brazilian food. JAMES What are the classics? SCODELARIO Rice and beans. But proper beans. JAMES What’s the most complex Brazilian dish to make? SCODELARIO Feijoada takes a good few hours. JAMES What is that? SCODELARIO It’s really good, and I’ll do it for you when we get back. It’s got, like, pork trotters and pig ear and everything —— JAMES Aw, poor piggy. SCODELARIO My son is a pescatarian, so I’ve been learning more vegetarian meals. But I don’t like bell peppers or chickpeas, and I think everything vegetarian is that. So I need better veggie recipes. Do you do Sunday dinners? Do you make the kids sit at the table with you? JAMES No. God, no, no, no. Growing up, it was pretty English. We had Sunday roasts. The Greek side, my grandfather’s side, we did a bit of Greek-y style but he wasn’t a big cook. SCODELARIO Do you ever have bacalhau? It’s salt cod. We do that for Easter, always. JAMES Do your kids — do they feel connected to the Brazilian part of you? SCODELARIO Yeah, I think food is a really great way of introducing kids to their culture and heritage and stuff. Because it’s something they can taste and see and be included in. He’s very proud of that. Both the kids are. Whenever we travel the world, the first thing I’ll do is find the local Brazilian restaurant. And luckily Brazilians are everywhere. What’s the biggest difference between craft service on a British film set versus an American one? JAMES We often talk about this. Basically, in England, craft doesn’t exist. SCODELARIO It doesn’t exist. They don’t feed us. JAMES It’s like a table with a kettle. And some terrible biscuits. SCODELARIO Crappy biscuits. Off brand. The cheap ones. JAMES A molding orange or something. Whereas here, in America, craft service is an art. SCODELARIO Incredible. It’s a whole truck, and anything you want they can just make. My favorite thing about working in America is the food on set. JAMES Not the work? SCODELARIO Not the work. [Both laugh] What are you eating, Kaya? On an American set? SCODELARIO Breakfast burrito, because that’s not a thing in England. I love a breakfast burrito. JAMES We should get one after this. SCODELARIO Yes, that’s exactly what we need. Jambalaya. I had that recently on a job, and I was like, that’s fun. Never had that before, that was great. It’s just that, every three hours, they will make sure there’s a hot meal for everyone. And we just don’t do that in the U.K. JAMES There’s a slight culture of Britishness where they’re like, “Oh, you don’t need — stop moaning!” It’s like a 14-hour day, and they’re like, “You can have a cup of tea!” SCODELARIO “Have a biscuit! You’re OK!” But we always, don’t we — we get for the crew, we’ll get, like, an ice cream truck or coffee. JAMES We’re good like that. SCODELARIO We’re good people. If you were a food dish, what would you be? Can you answer for each other? JAMES You would be — SCODELARIO A dehydrated mango. JAMES No, you would be six chicken nuggets. [Laughs] JAMES No, you would be something exotic with a simmering undertone of vermouth. SCODELARIO Ooh. All right, I’ll take it. You would be—— JAMES Some chips. SCODELARIO No, you would be something simple but delicious. Genuinely! Like this [burro e parmigiano]. You would be this. JAMES That’s what my ex-girlfriends used to say. SCODELARIO Easy, not overcomplicated. JAMES Simple but delicious. SCODELARIO A bit dumb but pretty. [Both laugh] Follow New York Times Cooking on Instagram, Facebook, YouTube, TikTok and Pinterest. item.title: A New Approach to Disaster Relief
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 3.53
Participants carrying Amazon’s portable rapid response technology systems during their disaster relief training exercise. (Photo: Pete Kiehart) From this summer’s intense wildfires to back-to-back earthquakes to a brewing Super El Niño, one thing is clear: The growing threat of natural disasters is hard to ignore. Supercharged by climate change, events like wildfires, earthquakes, hurricanes, and floods now occur more regularly, often in places that aren’t prepared for them. This reality means billions of people worldwide need stronger preparedness and resilience measures. This new era of heightened risk requires a new era of heightened response, from innovative tools to strong relationships to advanced preparation. Enter Amazon. “When I spoke with first responders, I kept hearing the same failures repeat over and over—disasters affecting their ability to communicate, provide relief quickly, or even access resources as basic as clean water,” said Jeffrey Schweitzer, Amazon’s disaster relief innovation lead. Along with nonprofit partners, Schweitzer and his team developed new, customizable rapid response technology systems to restore critical services, all in suitcase-sized packages that one person can carry and set up in just a few minutes. “During disasters, responders need to understand the landscape, the impact, where survivors are, and who needs help,” said Rodney Cooper, who serves as national director for technology and programs with the Information Technology Disaster Resource Center (ITDRC). “During Hurricane Helene, everything was dark. Survivors could not reach out to each other.” That’s exactly the kind of situation this new tech is made for: restoring services within hours, so communities don’t have to wait weeks to call loved ones or turn the lights back on. Amazon’s rapid response tech includes 10-plus configurations that relief personnel can set up: solar microgrids, satellite Wi-Fi, water purification devices, even terrain-mapping drones. The drone systems alone can cost up to $250,000, but Amazon provides them to partners at no cost. And the tech is reusable: After a disaster response ends, nonprofits ship the systems back to Amazon for inspection, refurbishment, and restocking. Meaning one system can serve multiple communities, across multiple disasters. The systems can power hospitals, emergency shelters, fire departments, and community centers. A single system can keep a 50-bed hospital running for 72 hours or serve more than 2,600 hot meals—and they’ve already been crucial for restoring communities after recent disasters. Following the recent twin earthquakes in Venezuela, where telecommunications were completely severed near the epicenter in La Guaira, Amazon worked with nonprofit partners on the ground to deliver portable Wi-Fi systems to connect clinics, shelters, and community hubs. One system was placed on a car roof to create a movie night for kids. And in Jamaica, after Hurricane Melissa, portable solar batteries and satellite Wi-Fi units restored power and communications within minutes so doctors could coordinate patient care. Solar systems even allowed World Central Kitchen to power its food trucks and serve hot meals after dark. “For Amazon, preparedness means prepositioning. It’s having the people trained. It’s having everything from pallets of diapers to satellite communications ready to go,” said Abe Diaz, senior manager for disaster relief at Amazon. “That means the time it takes for the community to get back on their feet is shorter, and ultimately that means recovery time is shorter.” Amazon will make 2,000 of these systems available to nonprofit partners in 2027, with 800 ready to ship from the company’s disaster relief hub in Tennessee this hurricane season. Preparation also requires coordination and practice. At a recent training exercise in a small Maryland town, Amazon brought together two dozen organizations—including local fire and rescue, nonprofit partners, and government agencies—to practice how people, technology, and partnerships can work together to strengthen disaster response. Participants launched into a series of hands-on missions, including a river crossing into an isolated flood-affected community, a simulated search-and-rescue mission, and helicopter-assisted aid delivery. Each mission was designed to put Amazon’s rapid response technology to the test in real-world conditions and allow local communities, companies, and government agencies to get hands-on experience with both the tech and each other. “You don’t want everyone exchanging business cards and meeting each other in the middle of a disaster itself,” said Civil Affairs Major Alex Haseley, an emergency management specialist with the U.S. Army. “Events like this, we’re getting to meet each other, we’re building some trust, we’re figuring out how to contact each other on relatively short notice. Emergency management is such a magical mission: When people feel what it’s like to truly help a survivor, it’s like a drug and you want to keep doing it.” During a disaster, hot meals do more than sustain people—they restore dignity and normalcy when communities need it most. For the training exercise, nonprofit organization Operation BBQ Relief used Amazon’s technology systems to power hot-meal preparation for dozens of people, including police officers and firefighters who serve the town daily. “A lot of times, the last thing you’re thinking about is nourishing yourself—you’re worried about your home, belongings,” said Chris Huggins, head of logistics and inventory for Operation BBQ Relief. “Barbecue brings hope and comfort—you’ve never sat down to a plate of barbecue and been sad, y’know? Taking five minutes to share a hot meal with a loved one is like saying, ‘Hey, there’s gonna be a better tomorrow. You’re not alone, and we’re here for you.’ This groundbreaking tech is a natural evolution of Amazon’s commitment to aid global communities threatened by sudden disaster. Since 2017, Amazon has donated and delivered over 30 million emergency supplies to support communities impacted by more than 200 disasters globally. Amazon leverages the same logistics network, aviation capabilities, and cloud technology that power its day-to-day operations to deliver rapid aid to communities facing crisis. “When a major disaster strikes, every minute a community spends without power, clean water, or connectivity is critical,” Schweitzer said. “Amazon is uniquely positioned to repurpose our existing delivery network, fulfillment hubs, and tech capabilities to get essential aid where it’s needed in hours, so even when infrastructures fail, recovery can start sooner.” When disasters strike, Amazon uses the same strengths that get packages to doorsteps to bring critical aid where it’s needed, fast. Since 2017, Amazon has donated and delivered more than 30 million relief items to support communities impacted by 200-plus disasters worldwide. For more information, visit AboutAmazon.com.

A down jacket has multiple uses on a hiking or backpacking gear list. It can be used as an insulating midlayer on its own or under a shell, as a warm outer jacket when you're less active in camp, or as an adjunct to your sleeping bag/quilt at night. For hiking or backpacking, some down jackets better meet hikers' needs than others in terms of warmth-to-weight ratio, hood design, durability, and cost. With these factors in mind, here are the best three-season down jackets that we recommend across a variety of price points. Be sure to check out our feature recommendations below, so you can choose the right jacket for your needs. | Make / Model | Gender | Weight | Fill Power | |---|---|---|---| | Patagonia Down Sweater Hoodie | M \| F | 14.8 oz/420g | 800 | | Feathered Friends EOS Jacket | M \| F | 11.8 oz/335g | 900 | | Arcteryx Cerium Down Hoodie | M \| F | 11.9 oz/335g | 850 | | Katabatic Gear Tarn Jacket | M \| F | 10.6 oz/303g | 850 | | REI Magma 850 Down Hoodie | M \| F | 13.1 oz/354g | 850 | | Mtn Hardware Ghost Whisperer | M \| F | 8.8 oz/249g | 800 | | Outdoor Research Helium Down Hoodie | M \| F | 15.4 oz/459g | 800 | | Montbell Ex Light Down Anorak | Unisex | 7.6 oz/215g | 900 | | LL Bean UL 850 Down Jacket | M \| F | 16 oz/450g | 850 | | Cotopaxi Fuego Hooded Down Jacket | M \| F | 13 oz/367g | 800 | 1. Patagonia Down Sweater Hoodie 2. Feathered Friends EOS Jacket 3. Arc’teryx Cerium Down Hoodie 4. Katabatic Gear Tarn Jacket 5. REI Magma 850 Down Hoodie 6. Mountain Hardwear Ghost Whisperer Down Hoody 7. Outdoor Research Helium Down Hoodie 8. Montbell Ex Light Down Anorak 9. LL Bean UL 850 Down Jacket 10. Cotopaxi Fuego Hooded Down Jacket Down Hoodie and Jacket Buying Guide Down Hoodies, Jackets, Sweaters, Anoraks, and Parkas Manufacturer product names are applied inconsistently to lighter-weight down hoodies and jackets. In general, hoodies, sweaters, and anoraks weigh under one pound. Look for ones with hoods, as they provide the most head and neck insulation. When it comes to jackets, some are lightweight and some are heavier, designed for winter use in harsh conditions. You really have to look at the overall jacket weight to determine which is which. Anything up to or slightly over 16 oz will be good for transitional weather in spring or autumn down to freezing by itself or layered under a shell, while heavier jackets will be more appropriate for winter use. Parkas are almost always intended for very cold winter conditions and are too warm for active use when hiking. Sewn Thru vs Baffled Construction With very few exceptions, lightweight down jackets and hoodies use sewn-through construction rather than box-baffled construction because it is less expensive and labor-intensive to manufacture. With sewn-through construction, the front and back of the jacket are sewn together, creating a pocket that prevents the down insulation from shifting. However, warm air can leak through the needle holes, making the jacket slightly cooler. This is not the case with a box-baffled design, which is more prevalent on premium down parkas intended for colder temperatures. Hood Adjustment The hoods on many lightweight or ultralight down hoodies and jackets are quite rudimentary, with elasticized hood openings that may be too large to prevent cold drafts from entering around your ears. It depends on your head size and the specific jacket. Hoods that are 1-way adjustable have volume controls in the back that let you shrink the size of the hood to provide a better fit. Hoods with 2-way adjustability go a step further and add neck cords that let you size the opening to fit your face and block out drafts. Two-way adjustability is pretty rare on lightweight down jackets and hoodies, but it's a premium feature worth looking for. Down Fill Power Down fill powers, such as 700, 800, 850, or 900, measure the effectiveness and compressibility of down insulation – the higher the better. Now, 900- or 950-fill-power down is primo stuff and can add a lot of cost to a jacket while keeping it very lightweight, since it takes less down by weight to keep you warm. You can get the same warmth with a lower grade of down, like 800 or 850, but it takes more of it to keep you warm and adds a bit of weight to the jacket. However, don't dismiss 700 fill-power down jackets, especially if they include synthetic insulation in moisture-prone areas. The warmth difference isn't that significant, and while they'll be a bit heavier, they're ideal in wet climates. Down Fill Weight The fill weight of a down jacket or hoodie measures the amount of down it has, by weight. While this can be informative, a jacket's actual warmth depends on both the amount of insulation and its design, which makes it hard to compare jackets with different styles. Most lightweight jacket manufacturers don't document the amount of down in their jackets, which can make it hard to tell which will be warmer in active use. Waterproof Down Some manufacturers use down in their jackets that has been coated with a chemical formulation, called DownTek or Nikwax, to make it more moisture-resistant and help it dry faster when it gets damp or wet. Honestly, the jury is still out on whether these treatments make any difference to the insulation performance of the down. Some manufacturers believe it degrades insulation value, and others use it because it's considered a desirable feature by prospective customers. SectionHiker never accepts payment for gear reviews or editorial coverage. When you buy through affiliate links on our site, we may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. Help us continue to test and write unsponsored and independent gear reviews, hiking and backpacking FAQs, and free hiking guides. I have a Patagonia down sweater. I wish it were a bit warmer sitting around at camp when it gets down to 20-30F. Is there a jacket you think would perform better for those situations? I think the REI magma 850, the Katabatic gear Tarn of FF Eos will get you down to 20. Thanks, Philip. Those are ones that seemed like they might fit the bill from warmth standpoint to me. FF and Katabatic are impossible to try on without ordering. I’m on the husky side. The EOS seems like it might be too athletic cut for me. I’ve tried on a Magma. 2XL is a bit big, but XL is snug. It looks like the Tarn XXL might be kind of in between from the size charts. Does that sound about right based on your experience I’m a large – no idea about how those other sizes fit As a jacket nerd, I think that down has really been overtaken by synthetic at this point. Anything sewn through will be far colder than continuous sheets of Primaloft/Polartec that you can sweat in and throw in the wash without concern. For deep cold, baffles + the compressibility of down starts to shine again. But 1) I wouldn’t wear any of these jackets for activities where I might sweat through them. Use fleece and a wind shirt or soft shell instead. 2) Polartec/Primaloft is still only equivalent to 550 down fill power in heat retention so jackets with it have to be heavier to compensate for the lack of heat retaining loft compared to down. 3) If you’re worried about sewn through pin holes buy box baffled jackets. But I’d worry a lot more about #2 above. EX down anorak is pretty much impossible to find. And discontinued. Why would you include that? What are you talking about? Montbell has them in stock . Based on the buying guide’s point about two-way hood adjustability being a rare premium feature, I’m curious how much it actually matters compared with a good one-way hood on a jacket like the Feathered Friends EOS. The commenter asking about staying warm at camp around 20-30F seems like the exact use case where that neck adjustment and overall fill weight would matter most. Many fixed-size hoods are simply sized too large, largely because the outdoor industry thinks that there are more climbers or downhill skiers who buy gear than hikers. Without two-way adjustability (neck cords) you might as well not be wearing the hood.

item.title: The other side of Croatia: ‘a landscape that could out-Tuscany Tuscany’
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 4.18
‘You’re going to Samobor? You must try kremšnita,” my Dubrovnik friends told me before I set off on my trip north. “But I’ve already had kremšnita in Zagreb,” I told them. They do it better in Samobor, they insisted. I wasn’t about to get embroiled in a battle of the cream cakes in a region where Croatians, Slovenes and Austrians all like to celebrate their own versions of this decadently thick, fat custard slice topped with puff pastry and icing sugar. But I was more than willing – happy, even – to follow everyone’s suggestions to try kremšnita in Hotel Livadić’s Kavana Livadić, in Samobor’s main King Tomislav Square, a mere half-hour drive west of Zagreb. It lived up to the hype – delicately rich, creamy and with a light touch. After spending a few weeks in sun-bleached Venetian Dalmatia, amid the scrubby, limestone Dinaric Alps, I had swapped empires and was firmly in Habsburg Croatia. Here, in Zagreb County’s prettiest town, handsome baroque houses in pastel shades of buttery yellow, apricot and pistachio, festooned with stucco, line narrow King Tomislav Square, whose umbrella-shaded cafe terraces were filled with Croatians getting their morning fix of coffee and chatter. The lush green Samobor Hills overlook the medieval town, through which the Gradna – part river, part stream – flows and ripples under wooden bridges adorned with flowers. One of these bridges led to the onion-domed church of Saint Anastasia; another, with a fairytale wooden roof, took me to one of Samobor’s many green spaces, dotted with free red deckchairs, which had the slogan “Volim Samobor” (“I love Samobor”) written in white. In front of them, the stately former home (now the town’s museum) of one of Croatia’s foremost 19th-century composers, Ferdo Livadić, added to the air of gentle refinement, of culture worn lightly. It was easy to visualise Livadić entertaining his artistic friends, including Franz Liszt, in this august setting. As well as the graceful architectural legacy of the Austro-Hungarian monarchy, this rolling green landscape is crisscrossed with forested trails, particularly within the Žumberak nature park, about 16 miles (26km) west of Samobor, where weekenders from Zagreb come to hike and bike in woods of hornbeam, oak and beech with bubbling waterfalls. Not having time for a full-on hike, I could still drive to Potočna dolina Slapnica, near the Vranjak waterfalls, and scramble up the path beside a series of cascades each more impressive than the last. Closer to Samobor, the hilltop ruins of Okić castle rose to nearly 500m above sea level, one of the best-preserved romanesque fortifications in the country. The Mongols couldn’t defeat it, nor could the Ottoman Turks. Sadly, it defeated me when I attempted to hike to the top. Not realising there was a newer, easier path, I ended up on one that was little else but vertical tree roots. With a newly healed ankle and no phone signal, I thought it unwise to continue. But it’s on my list for next time. A much easier path to take was along the Plešivica wine road, where more than three dozen wineries were scattered on a heart-shaped route between the village of Plešivica (10 miles south-west of Samobor) and the town of Jastrebarsko. In a harmonious landscape that could out-Tuscany Tuscany, vineyards clung to steep slopes between forested hills, many producing the sparkling wine Plešivica is renowned for. I met Martina and Krešimir Ivančić, whose ancestors were given a noble title and coat of arms by the Austrian empress Maria Theresa in 1759. The griffin on the family crest inspired the name of the Griffin Winery, which came about when a Hungarian count gave them a licence to plant a vineyard in 1773. Martina took me to the covered patio of a wooden hut above the vineyards, a suitably bucolic place to taste an elegant and lightly fruity sparkling rose made from red portugieser grapes. We carried on in the extremely stylish tasting room, where plates of cured meats and cheeses accompanied glasses of full-bodied chardonnay. I was also offered copanjek, a thin savoury pastry pie of cheese and greens. “They’re very portable, so workers would take them to the vineyard,” Martina told me. This looked like the winemaker’s version of rudarska greblica, which I had tasted that morning in the village of Rude, about a 10-minute drive west of Samobor, and liked so much I had to have two. Filled with cheese and walnuts, carrots or greens, these used to be made by the wives of Rude’s long-gone miners. They’re such an integral part of the region that they have their own festival every July and have been given EU protected status. At Pekarnica Nikl, in Rude, I met Jelena and Andrejas Nikl, the only authorised bakers of this much adored speciality. Jelena acknowledged the responsibility of keeping up this tradition of rudarska greblica, especially with the paperwork that came with legal protection – but, she said, it was worth it. All around the Samobor Hills, people were holding fast to their heritage and infusing it with life. The Korak family is one of the most illustrious, with its Michelin-starred Korak winery and restaurant in Plešivica. Not a whiff of Michelin stuffiness or pretentiousness here, just the fourth and fifth generations of a family producing superb wine and making beautiful food in a serene setting facing the vineyards. Brother Bernard is chef (and has worked with Massimo Bottura of Italy’s Osteria Francescana and Ana Roš of Slovenia’s Hiša Franko); sister Vera is front of house; and parents Velimir and Mirjana tend the vines – even the siblings’ grandparents are still making cheese and pršut (prosciutto) for the restaurant. Bernard grows as much as he can – the rest comes from local producers, including the farmer whose pigs are fed on scraps from Bernard’s kitchen. And if it’s not in season, it’s not on the plate. My June visit rewarded me with a truffle tagliatelle, and clams and green beans in a caviar sauce, among other delicious dishes in a five-course tasting menu at €118 (a very reasonable price, and in keeping with the region’s overall lower prices). I could only imagine what delights autumn will bring, especially during the annual Wine Days festival in Jastrebarsko from 25-27 September. The Samobor Hills will be teeming with autumn truffles and mushrooms, and welcoming the change in season the best way they know – on the plate.
