item.title: The ultimate guide to Delta One Suites
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 6.10
The ultimate guide to Delta One Suites It's hard to believe it has been 10 years since Delta wowed the travel industry as the first airline in the world to unveil an all-suite business-class cabin with each seat having its own closing door for privacy. Since then, Delta One Suites has won the TPG Award for best U.S. airline business class several times as well. No wonder these enclosed pod styles have become more popular with airlines, including Qatar Airways, British Airways, Virgin Atlantic, All Nippon Airways and Air France, among others. Here's what you need to know about Delta One Suites, where you can find them and how you can use miles to book them. Aircraft with Delta One Suites You can find Delta One Suites aboard the following planes in Delta's fleet (and you can check out our reviews of each): Although the product on the 767 is not technically a true Delta One Suite due to the lack of a sliding door, we'll include it for the purposes of this article, since these seats' footprint matches that of the suites aboard the A350 and A330-900neo. These are the long-haul jets that do not have Delta One Suites: - Airbus A330-300 - Airbus A330-200 - Boeing 767-300ER However, Delta will begin retrofitting its aging A330s with Delta One Suites starting later this year. We do not yet know how long this rollout will take altogether, though. The airline also recently announced that it will introduce all-new Delta One Suites aboard its forthcoming Airbus A350-1000s, which it plans to take delivery of starting in 2027, so be on the lookout for those. That's a lot of information, so it's important to pay attention to what kind of jet is operating your flight. According to Airfleets.net, the airline has the following numbers of each jet, and this is the total number of Delta One suites you'll find aboard each. | Aircraft type | Number in fleet | Number of seats | |---|---|---| | Airbus A350-900 | 41 | 32-40 depending on configuration | | Airbus A330-900neo | 39 | 29 | | Boeing 767-400ER | 21 | 34 | | Airbus A330-330 (refit project) | 11 | Being refitted | | Airbus A330-200 (refit project) | 31 | Being refitted | | Airbus A350-1000 | 20 on order, deliveries begin 2027 | 53 | While seat counts vary on the A350, all the A330-900neos have 29 Delta One Suites and all retrofitted 767s have 34 suites. On all of them except the A350-900s with 40 seats, Delta One is in a single cabin at the front of the aircraft, so your experience should be pretty similar from plane to plane. For those interested, the forthcoming A350-1000s will also have a large front cabin with 45 of the new Delta One Suites as well as a small back section with just eight of them. Delta primarily flies the A350, A330-900neo to an array of destinations in Africa, Asia, Europe and Australia from its various hubs, including: - Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL) - Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport (DTW) - John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) - Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) - Minneapolis-St. Paul International Airport (MSP) - Salt Lake City International Airport (SLC) - Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) It tends to operate the 767-400 on shorter transatlantic routes between the East Coast and Europe. What to expect with Delta One Suites What makes the Delta One Suites so special? These are staggered Vantage XL seats, so each has a large footprint and plenty of privacy, especially those with closing doors aboard the A350 and A330-900neo. Each is around 20 1/2 inches wide and up to 77 inches long in bed mode on the A350. On the A330-900neo, they are 22 1/2 inches wide and up to 80 inches long. The 767 has the smallest seats, with only 20 inches in width, and a bed that's 77 inches long. All recline to fully lie-flat beds with memory foam cushions. The suites on the A350 and A330-900neo are very similar, though there are some slight design differences that those with a keen eye will notice. Here's a quick look at the differences between these planes and their onboard features. | Plane | A350-900 | A330-900neo | 767-400 | |---|---|---|---| | Total Delta One Suites | 32-40 | 29 | 34 | | Configuration | 1-2-1 | 1-2-1 | 1-2-1 | | Seat dimensions | 20 1/2 inches wide, 76 to 77 inches lie-flat | 22 1/2 inches wide, 79 to 80 inches lie-flat | 20 inches wide, 77 inches lie-flat | | Screen size | 18 inches | 18 1/2 inches | 18 1/2 inches | We found the aisles on the A330-900neo to be a little cramped, though the Wi-Fi was fast. The A330-900neo, A350-900 with 40 seats and 767 have just two lavatories for business class, while the A350-900 with 32 Delta One seats has four lavatories. So, you might find lineups on some flights. Delta One seats on the retrofitted 767-400 do not have sliding doors, but they offer more privacy than their older counterparts on Delta's 767-300s and feature finishes that bring them in line with the newer A350s and A330-900neos. Delta One seat selection guide On all of the jets, the Delta One Suites are arranged in a staggered 1-2-1 configuration. The suites on the sides of the cabin alternate between being closer to the aisle and closer to the window. The "true window" seats have their wider armrest on the aisle side, which provides you with even more privacy. Though truth be told, I don't mind the other window seats that are closer to the aisle since the closing door offers enough privacy on its own, and it's easier to get in and out of them. The seats in the center of the cabin shift either to the right or to the left of the preceding row to maximize seat pitch. So you won't find "honeymoon" center seats that are closer together, like you'll see on some other airlines, like LATAM. Instead, there is always a wide armrest and a movable privacy screen between center seats, no matter which row you sit in. Here's a quick guide to which seats are best for which type of traveler. | Aircraft | True window seats | Best for travel companions | Seats to avoid | |---|---|---|---| | A350-900 (32 seats) | Rows 3, 5, 7 seats A and D | Any row B and C seats | 1B, 1C, 9B, 9C — near galley and lavatory | | A350-900 (40 seats) | Rows 3, 5, 7 seats A and D Row 10 seats A and D | Any row B and C seats | 1B, 1C, 9B, 9C — near galley and lavatory | | A330-900neo | Rows 2, 4, 6 seats A and J | Any row D and G seats | 8A — near galley | | 767-400ER | Rows 2, 4, 6, 8 seats A and D | Any row B and C seats | 9A, 9D — near galley and lavatory | Delta One seat features As you can see, Delta One Suites bear similar dimensions and layouts no matter which aircraft you find them on. The primary differences are the number of seats on each jet, the lavatory-to-passenger ratio, and the fact that the seats on the 767 lack actual doors. Other than that, the experience is pretty consistent. The suites have 18 to 18 1/2-inch high-resolution touchscreens, high-powered USB ports for charging your devices and universal power outlets. Passengers can illuminate "Do not disturb" indicators, adjust their own lighting and take advantage of numerous personal stowage areas. Business-class travelers can enjoy hallmark Delta soft touches, including amenity kits (the current ones are cute Missoni designs with Grown Alchemist skincare products), over-ear headphones and and Missoni bedding that includes a mattress pad, lightweight duvet and memory foam pillow. Menus created by celebrity chefs like José Andrés, which you can conveniently preorder and wines chosen by the airline's sommelier, Andrea Robinson, are all presented with the airline's Alessi glassware, plates and cutlery, lending the meal service an elevated ambience. Finding Delta One award tickets Since Delta stopped publishing award charts and switched to a dynamic pricing model for award tickets several years back, it has become harder and harder to find decently priced award tickets in Delta One. Long-haul flights can cost several hundred thousand miles in each direction. For the most part, Delta prices long-haul flights in suites at exorbitant levels, ranging from 125,000 to around 800,000 miles each way. Yes, you read that correctly. That said, you can still find some rare saver-level awards — including recent deals between various U.S. hubs and cities across Europe starting at 115,000 Delta SkyMiles. I also tend to find that awards on the airline's flights between Seattle and Taipei are priced lower than on its other transpacific routes. Delta has a few useful award-search tools that make finding award prices easier. You can use the flexible dates calendar on Delta's website to look for awards five weeks at a time. And if you're just searching routes where you know an A330-900neo, A350 or 767 with suites is in service, select the option for nonstop flights to narrow down your query quickly. You might also look at city pairs that pass through non-hubs, since some of these options will be available at lower fares and mileage prices. On dates when you see noticeably less-expensive awards than surrounding days, you might be able to book them using partner currencies like Air France-KLM Flying Blue miles or Virgin Atlantic Flying Club points. Don't forget to use tools like Seats.aero to search broad swaths of the calendar. With a paid subscription, you can even use search filters like operating airline (Delta) and program you want to use miles from, including Delta's own SkyMiles frequent flyer program and those of its partners. Using points and miles to book Delta One Suites If you want to use miles to book Delta One Suites, you have a few choices. Delta SkyMiles First, you could use Delta's own SkyMiles. The program is a 1:1 transfer partner of American Express Membership Rewards if you have a card like American Express Platinum Card® or the American Express® Gold Card. Or, consider applying for one of Delta's cobranded credit cards to rack up award miles quickly both on welcome offers and everyday spending (terms apply): Virgin Atlantic Flying Club Virgin Atlantic Flying Club is a Delta partner and uses dynamic pricing, so it's harder to find bargains using Flying Club points for Delta One award tickets. However, it's easy to rack up Virgin Atlantic points since Flying Club is a transfer partner of every major transferable points program, including: - American Express Membership Rewards (at a 1:1 ratio) - Bilt (at a 1:1 ratio) - Capital One (at a 1:1 ratio) - Chase Ultimate Rewards (at a 1:1 ratio) - Citi ThankYou Rewards (at a 1:1 ratio) - Wells Fargo Rewards (at a 1:1 ratio) - Marriott Bonvoy (at a 3:1 ratio, with a 5,000-point bonus for transferring 60,000 points; expect a 48-hour transfer time) That said, you'll likely have to redeem well over 100,000 points in each direction (and sometimes much more than that), depending on where you want to fly. Air France-KLM Flying Blue Another good option is Flying Blue. This program is a transfer partner of: - American Express Membership Rewards - Bilt - Chase Ultimate Rewards - Capital One - Citi ThankYou Rewards - Wells Fargo Rewards There are two major caveats, though. First, availability for awards booked through partners is very scarce. Second, you will typically pay more taxes and surcharges on these tickets than you will when using Delta SkyMiles. Downsides to Delta One Delta One has won the TPG Award for best U.S. airline business class several times, but there are a few drawbacks to be aware of before you actually fly: - Award availability at affordable mileage levels is extremely limited. - The suites are consistent but do vary slightly by aircraft type. - Many Europe and South America routes are operated by planes without suite-style seats. - The food, while elevated, does not always impress. - The number of lavatories does not feel sufficient for the number of passengers on some planes. - Newer suites will be coming online with the advent of the Airbus A350-1000, so you might want to wait for those. Bottom line Delta changed the game with its all-suites business class a decade ago. Closing doors (on the A350s and A330-900neos), up-to-the-minute tech and signature soft amenities all ensure a comfortable and memorable flight on the airline's newest Delta One products. However, the exorbitant award pricing of many flights with these suites means they're out of reach for most flyers looking to redeem miles to book them (except at the most inconvenient of times). Delta adds another new city from LAX, bolsters 7 others as hub battle intensifies For the second time in less than a week, Delta Air Lines announced it's adding a service to Los Angeles. The Atlanta-based carrier on Friday announced a new nonstop route from Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) to Philadelphia International Airport (PHL). The daily flight will launch next summer. That news comes just days after TPG reported that Delta planned to launch a new route from LA to California's Central Coast, where it will return after a 19-year hiatus. It's part of a larger buildup the carrier is undertaking in Southern California. Additional daily flights on 7 existing routes In addition to the new service to Philly and Monterey unveiled this week, Delta on Friday also announced plans to bolster schedules on seven existing routes. Beginning next spring, the carrier will add additional daily flights on its LA routes to seven cities: Boston, Cincinnati, Houston, Raleigh, San Antonio, San Diego and Seattle. All told, Delta expects to fly its biggest schedule ever in LA next year, the carrier told TPG. "We're creating more opportunities for customers to connect to the places they want to go while building on our long-term commitment to Los Angeles and the West," Amy Martin, vice president of network planning, said in a statement. Delta's largest schedule yet in Los Angeles Even prior to Friday's expansion, the carrier had been on pace to grow its total departures at LAX by roughly 9% during the first half of next year, according to data from aviation analytics firm Cirium. It has been a busy year for Delta at its Southern California hub. Since last winter, the carrier has launched new long-haul services to Hong Kong and Melbourne. In July, Delta announced a new route to Manila, Philippines. In November, it'll bring back LA service to Vancouver for the first time in eight years. And the carrier just opened its second business-class-only Delta One Lounge at LAX, following massive terminal investments at the airport in recent years. Hub battle heats up Still, Los Angeles remains one of America's most competitive cities when it comes to air travel. Each of the "Big Three" U.S. carriers (Delta, along with American Airlines and United Airlines) has a hub at LAX. Delta will offer more flights from LAX than any other carrier this year, per Cirium. But United has a bigger Pacific schedule from the airport — and will grow its long-haul offerings at LAX in 2027 with new service to Osaka, Japan. "It's a very competitive marketplace, and we're in it to win it as well," United chief commercial officer Andrew Nocella said on the airline's July earnings call. item.title: Maintenance delay? Airlines may soon have fewer reasons to compensate you
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 3.13
Maintenance delay? Airlines may soon have fewer reasons to compensate you Flight delayed or canceled? For airline passengers, it's already an uphill battle to get any sort of compensation. Soon, travelers may have even fewer protections. The U.S. Department of Transportation just finalized a rule that could make it harder for flyers to get a free meal or a hotel voucher when their travel plans get upended by a dreaded maintenance issue. The change, which alters how the government views maintenance delays, was ordered by a federal law passed in 2024. It's set to take effect in October. Once it does, airlines could face less pressure to pay up when flights are delayed due to mechanical problems. That means passengers could be on the hook to pay for whatever expenses pile up while they're stuck. Let's take a look at what's changing, why this is happening, and how you can protect your wallet when you fly in the future. It's already a hurdle to get compensated for flight delays Already, passengers are often out of luck when flight delays and cancellations pop up. Airlines typically don't pay for stranded flyers' expenses when bad weather or air traffic control problmes lead to flight woes. Those disruptions are typically considered outside the airline's control. Maintenance has historically been different. Up until now, the DOT has generally counted those delays and cancellations as within the airline's control. And when it's the airline's "fault," carriers will often pay for passengers' costs like meals, hotel accommodations and ground transportation. But will airlines be as generous in the future? That's the big question. Rule change in October Next month, the DOT will change its approach to aircraft maintenance delays and cancellations. Starting Oct. 19, unexpected maintenance that can't wait until after the flight will generally not count as "controllable." That means airlines could be free to stop offering meals and hotel accommodations for some flight delays — even if the delay is due to maintenance. In its final rule, the Trump administration was clear on what this shift will likely mean for passengers: "The number of delays and cancellations for which air carriers provide amenities and compensation to consumers is expected to be reduced," the DOT said. Not just maintenance The changes don't only apply to maintenance-related disruptions, by the way. Several other types of flight delays and cancellations will no longer count as something within the airline's "control." Some examples include when a plane has to be cleaned because a passenger has died on board, when an unruly flyer has to be removed, and cyber attacks (as long as the airline has been up to date with all cybersecurity regulations). Why is this happening? This new rule was actually mandated by the 2024 Federal Aviation Administration Reauthorization, which was passed by Congress and signed into law by former President Joe Biden. Ironically, that bill was notable for strengthening some consumer protections, beefing up airline refund rules. Those policies will remain as-is. Read more: Getting a refund for a canceled or delayed flight: What to know in 2026 But passengers will likely be less enthusiastic about this latest shift, which could leave travelers with fewer options for reimbursement when they are stranded. Not all maintenance delays Airlines won't be off the hook for all maintenance disruptions. These changes would only apply to unexpected mechanical problems that pop up outside carriers' scheduled maintenance programs. Essentially, we're talking about issues that must be fixed before departure, often for safety reasons. Airlines would still be considered responsible for more routine maintenance disruptions, the DOT tells TPG. And when those snafus happen, carriers would still have to meet their customer service promises listed at FlightRights.gov. What airlines are saying We should also note: Airlines haven't technically said they will scale back on paying for hotels and meals. But it appears they'll have much more flexibility in deciding whether to compensate passengers. Airline industry officials argue that carriers aggressively compete for customers, and continue to offer customer service policies that go beyond what the government requires. Another point Supporters also argue these changes will improve government data on flight disruptions. In the future, federal regulators — and consumers — will get a clearer picture of why flights are delayed or canceled. What should travelers do? Going forward, the best way for passengers to protect themselves is likely to keep a travel insurance policy or use a credit card with built-in protections. Certain cards, for instance, carry trip delay policies that can help flyers recoup unexpected costs when they run into flight woes. Just keep in mind that to make a successful claim, you typically have to book your whole trip with that card. Oh, and of course, keep all your receipts. Bottom line This is the latest blow to airline consumer protections. Last year, the Trump administration scuttled a Biden-era proposal that would have required carriers to offer cash compensation to flyers when "controllable" flight issues occur. Now, under this congressionally mandated change, passengers may find it harder to even get a free meal when they're delayed. Related reading: FAQ Yes. The airline may (or may not) give you anything, but you can always ask. Keep in mind that some maintenance delays will still be considered "controllable." And in those cases, your carrier may still owe you special accommodations, such as a meal or a hotel room. Yes. Federal refund rules aren't changing. Airlines must offer a full refund if your flight is canceled or significantly delayed. The catch: You're only owed a refund if you don't actually fly. Here's more on how refunds work. No. Every airline has different "guarantees" they offer to stranded passengers. You can find those promises at the U.S. Department of Transportation's FlightRights.gov dashboard. Keep in mind, those guarantees only apply when the cancellation or delay is within the airline's "control. And with these changes in October, fewer flight disruptions will be considered "controllable."

Citi / AAdvantage Executive vs. Globe: 2 great options for American Airlines fans Editor's Note The Citi® / AAdvantage® Globe™ Mastercard® (see rates and fees) and Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard® (see rates and fees) are closely-competing cards aimed at American Airlines enthusiasts. Their annual fees — $350 and $695, respectively — are far enough apart to make it important to carefully consider which option is best for you. If you're going to spend an extra $345 each year on a card, you want to make sure you're getting at least as much value as you're paying for. You should get the AAdvantage Globe if you often fly American but aren't loyal to the airline, while the AAdvantage Executive is at its most powerful in the hands of a dedicated American Airlines loyalist. Since both cards earn AAdvantage miles, offer some level of Admirals Club access and provide day-of-travel perks for American Airlines, we'll need to dig deep into the details to highlight why each card fits specific types of travelers. The AAdvantage Globe is the way to go if you're looking for an AAdvantage card for your everyday spending, as it offers more bonus categories than the Executive card.
